5d7ce667-91be-5456-a2b0-7cd880b231f3.name: *Portrait of Ruđer Bošković*
5d7ce667-91be-5456-a2b0-7cd880b231f3.description:
In this portrait world-famed Croatian scientist Ruđer Bošković (1711–1787) is 45 years of age as stated in the legend under the painting. Seen in his study, with his published works arranged on a shelf, he sits in an armchair, at his desk, dressed in the Jesuit uniform of black cassock and a cap. In his right hand, he holds compasses while his left hand rests on a planetarium; his face looks out to the observer. The colours have an overall brown tone and the portrait is faithful, though of only mediocre quality. Painted by an unknown Italian painter, Bošković was teaching mathematics in Rome at the time.  
Beneath the portrait is an inscription in Latin:  
P.ROGERIUVS BOSCOVICH S.I.IN COLLEGIO ROM.MAT. PROFES.  
NATUS RAGUSIJ XV KAL. IVNIJ MDCCXI AETATIS ANNO XLV  
Bošković was a leading physicist, mathematician, astronomer, philosopher and writer. Born in Dubrovnik, he was educated at the Jesuit college there and then in Rome. In 1725, he entered the Society of Jesus and remained in it until its dissolution in 1773. He was a professor at many schools and universities throughout Italy and travelled throughout Europe. A member of many academies, he published numerous scientific works. He was an all-round intellectual that studied and taught archaeology, literature, philosophy and rhetoric, and, in addition, worked as a diplomat. At the end of his life, his mental health suffered, and he died completely exhausted from pneumonia in 1773.
5d7ce667-91be-5456-a2b0-7cd880b231f3.short_description:
A portrait of the world-famed Croatian scientist, Ruđer Bošković (1711–1787), painted in the mid-18th century by an unknown artist. The portrait shows him sitting in his study surrounded by the many books he wrote and clad in the habit of the Jesuits. In his right hand, he holds compasses while his left hand rests on a planetarium. According to the legend at the bottom of the painting, the portrait dates to 1756 when Bošković was teaching mathematics in Rome aged 45.  
This leading physicist, mathematician, astronomer, philosopher and writer, born in Dubrovnik, educated at the Jesuit college there and then in Rome, entered the Society of Jesus in 1725 and remained in it until its dissolution in 1773.
5d7ce667-91be-5456-a2b0-7cd880b231f3.holder: Museum of Icons of the Serbian Orthodox Church Community
5d7ce667-91be-5456-a2b0-7cd880b231f3.method_for_datation: According to a legend at the bottom of the painting, the painting portrays Bošković at the age of 45. Therefore, since he was born in 1711, the portrait dates to 1756.

5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.name: Church and Hospital of Misericórdia of Viana do Castelo
5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.description:
The Misericórdia of Viana do Castelo, hospital and church, is unique and unparalleled in Portugal. The main building served both as an administrative headquarters and a hospital, with the attached Church managed autonomously.  
A sober façade contrasting with an embellished interior equals a fine example of the notion of the Baroque *Gesamtkunstwerk*, “total work of art” in spite of its precise floor plan and single nave. *Azulejos* cover the nave walls, depicting biblical scenes representing the 14 Acts of Mercy. In the central arch, a large panel depicts Our Lady of Mercy. The chancel is also ornamented with *azulejos* representing scenes from the Life of the Virgin Mary and Jesus. The *Grotesco* paintings on the ceiling by Manuel Gomes depict the *Holy Trinity*, *Assumption of Our Lady* and *Escape into Egypt*.  
Ambrósio Coelho carved the gilded wooden retable and the side altars, which are crowned by a gilded pelmet. An Iberian organ is placed in the High Choir.
5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.short_description: The Church of the Misericórdia of Viana do Castelo has a sober façade that contrasts with its embellished interior. It is a fine example of the Baroque *Gesamtkunstwerk*, “total work of art”: the chancel and the nave walls are covered with *azulejos* (painted tile panels) signed by Policarpo de Oliveira Bernardes, creating a masterly mix with the *Grotesco* paintings of the ceiling and the gilded wooden altarpieces.
5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.type: Religious, church, hospital and administrative buildings
5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.method_for_datation: Historical documents from the District Archive of Misericódia of Viana do Castelo

5eb0b404-01ef-5d13-a8dc-78064643ffb0.history: The Confraria da Misericórdia of Viana do Castelo was established in 1523 by formal request of its Council and deferred by the King. Its headquarters and chapel were built in the square close to the town walls, nowadays called Praça da República. Almost in ruins in 1557, the building was rebuilt according to the drawings of João Jácome Luna and clearly inspired by Italian *loggia*s. In 1714, the chapel being once more in a poor condition, a new renovation plan of the interior was commissioned by the Brotherhood to Manuel Pinto de Vila Lobos, a military engineer. Starting in 1716, reconstruction work finished eight years later. By a decree, dated 16 June 1910, the Church together with the hospital, were classified National Monuments.

606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.name: *Still life with Crabs, Pitcher, Glass, Loaf and Mouse*
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.description:
Izbighy Veres of Kassa (Košice) was one of the most accomplished painters of the period in Hungary. According to sources, he executed several commissions in Kassa (Košice), and a number of his still life paintings are in Slovakian and Hungarian collections today. Indications of the Hungarian origins of this painting are evident not only in the signature, but also in the blue-white lead-glazed jar; in addition, the loaf of bread is similar to that seen on a supraport painting by him in Koháry Castle at Szentantal (Antol). In another painting in the Xantus János Museum, Győr, Izbighy arranged a heap of crawfish on a plate in a similar way.  
Up until the beginning of the 20th century, discussion of Izbighy Veres' still life paintings was primarily in terms of their symbolic meaning. In this particular painting, however, this is hardly a major consideration as, clearly, it is influenced by the 17th-century still life genre of Austria and south Italy and, considering its style and spirituality, is certainly related to three works of the Austrian “Burgher paintress” Anna Maria Punz (Österreichische Galerie, Vienna), though this one by Izbighy is of an earlier date.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.short_description: The signed work of István Izbighy (Izbigi) Veres, a painter from Kassa (Košice) shows the influence of Austrian and south Italian still life painting, in particular the work of the “Burgher paintress” Anna Maria Punz. His other works may well have symbolic meaning but symbolism is a minor consideration when considering this particular painting.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and the date established by stylistic analysis.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.obtention: Transferred in an exchange from a Swiss private collection to a private collection in Karinthia, Austria.

66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.name: *St. Mary Magdalene*
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.description:
The altarpiece has a semi-circular top edge and shows the figure of St. Mary Magdalene placed in a shallow diagonal in the mid-ground behind step-like stone blocks. She is wearing a dress with long, wide, slightly flattened and relaxed folds and with her head thrown back, she is casting a repentant look at the sky, her hands around a large Crucifix. The scene, which takes place in a forest with a cave, has Mary Magdalene kneeling upon and leaning against natural stone blocks. Her other attributes are a whip with five lashes, a pot of ointment, a skull and an open book. The colours are muted and in many places dark, with an accent of light only on Magdalene's breast, face and hands and on the two angels' heads that peep from the cloud above the rounded cave opening.  
*St. Mary Magdalene,* commissioned by the boot-makers' guild to hang above an altarpiece in St. Mary's Church in Zagreb, was the work of Anton Cebej, who besides Valentin Metzinger, Franjo Ilovšek and Fortunato Bergant was one of the most respected Slovenian painters of the time. Three years later, in 1773, the cobblers' guild commissioned a painting from him for an altarpiece, which depicts the Death of St. Joseph.  
Cebej was particularly distinguished in religious compositions and portraits, and among his contemporaries, his style is closest to the Italian model. The professional crafts guilds of the same or different professions had a very strong humanitarian and religious component, and to express their religious obligations some guilds had their own altars of which they took permanent care, such as the guilds of Zagreb's Gradec already mentioned.  
Removed during renovation of the church, the altars and paintings became the property of collector Solomon Berger, founder of the Ethnographic Museum in Zagreb. The Museum of Arts and Crafts on several occasions bought or was donated pieces from his collection.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.short_description: *St. Mary Magdalene,* commissioned by the boot-makers' guild to hang above an altarpiece they had also commissioned for St. Mary's in Zagreb, was painted by Anton Cebej, one of the most influential Slovenian painters of his time, distinguished in religious compositions and portraits. Among his contemporaries, Cebej's style is closest to the Italian model.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.initial_owner: The painting hung above the altarpiece in St. Mary’s Church, Zagreb until 1908.
66a80969-9e6e-5ff5-84fa-b05805576bf2.method_for_datation: In the bottom right-hand corner, on the edge of the open page of the book is the signature “17 Antonius Zebey F.70.”

66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.name: Bureau cabinet for the display of porcelain
66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.description:
A tripartite-body bureau cabinet with varied veneering, it has a chest of drawers at the bottom with three wavy fronted drawers; a bureau with a fall-front in the middle, and a glazed top section with doors that shut onto an interior lined in green silk, with shaped, carved, gilded shelves and consoles to display porcelain.  
While the design for this type of furniture is typical of Venetian production, its purpose reflects contemporary European enthusiasm for the Far East and its art, especially porcelain and lacquer. Although lacquer and porcelain objects were imported into Europe, craftsmen there attempted to master the techniques of lacquer production, and the first European porcelain factories were opened around this time. The popularity of these wares resulted in special porcelain and lacquer display halls in mansions and palaces and the use of bureau cabinets such as this one.
66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.short_description: A tripartite-body bureau cabinet with varied veneering, the top section consists of a carved gilded structure with consoles for displaying porcelain closed by a double glazed door. The bureau’s purpose reflects contemporary European enthusiasm for the Far East and its art, especially porcelain and lacquer, which resulted in special porcelain and lacquer display halls in mansions and palaces and the use of bureau cabinets such as this one.

676840b7-fa48-530f-8796-1f2f216489c5.name: *Quart*
676840b7-fa48-530f-8796-1f2f216489c5.description:
The *quart* is derived from an old Czech unit of volume of approximately 1.4 litres. The jug is decorated with a typical segmented strip with roses, and a central area featuring a landscape with fortified towns and a rider. Folk art characteristically disregarded the natural scale. For example, although it is in the background, the dovecote on the right is the same size as the spire of what appears to be a chateau.  
The shape and decoration of the object are based on Rococo faience following the tradition of Habán ceramics. The Habáns were Anabaptists driven out of Tyrol in the 16th century. They found refuge in Moravia – which was religiously tolerant at the time – and its clayey soil provided quality material for the production of faience. The Habáns had to leave Moravia after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 and many of them settled in adjacent territory of western Slovakia, where they gradually became assimilated into the local Catholic population. Some of the Habán potters returned to Moravia in the last quarter of the 17th century to practice their craft under more favourable conditions. The tradition of “folk faience” in Moravia goes back to this period.  
Jan Neumayer was said to have come from Pisa, but it is likely he only trained in Italy. He was one of the artists of the Olomouc workshop which, together with a counterpart in Šternberk, developed the folk faience tradition. The motifs of horse riders were frequently derived from J. Ridinger's engravings, many of which adorned chateau interiors. Ceramic and glass vessels sometimes featured production dates and the names of their owners, indicating that their manufacture was perhaps prompted by a “souvenir” value. Their ornamentation of multi-coloured floral patterns is found on folk ceramics and costumes to this day.

The shape and decoration of the object are based on Rococo faience following the tradition of Habán ceramics. The multi-coloured floral pattern may be found on folk ceramics and costumes to this day.

677db211-c58d-50b1-b232-635d73f3327c.name: Coolers for glasses
677db211-c58d-50b1-b232-635d73f3327c.description:
A pair of bulgy coolers with short, broad, ringed necks topped by deep crenellations in the form of crowns. They show traces of side handles that are now broken off. The body bears the Sampaio e Melo coat of arms, painted in underglaze cobalt blue and overglaze iron red, green and gold enamels. As had happened with pieces commissioned by the Portuguese in the 16th and 17th centuries, the Chinese potters interpreted emblems and the coat of arms in their own way transforming a heraldic element, the lambrequin, for example, into a strictly decorative, complex arabesque drawing. The rest of the decoration is made up of sprays of flowers in Chinese *imari* colours (underglaze cobalt blue, and overglaze iron-red and gold) and floral borders.  
The shape was probably inspired by an English silver cooler known as a monteith, which had a removable mount adapted at the top, allowing for the cooling of both bottles and, with the mount in place, glasses. The name Monteith, according to some authors, refers to an eccentric Scottish gentleman, “M. Monteith”, the hem of whose kilt was said to have been indented in the same fashion as the monteith. Other authors present Delft faience from the Netherlands as a possible source of inspiration.  
The commission of these vessels have been attributed to members of different Portuguese families, namely Manuel Corte Real de Sampaio from the 5th Government Council of India (1668–1671); Francisco José de Sampaio Melo e Castro, 66th Governor and 40th Viceroy to India from 1720 to 1723; and to the noble family Melo Sampaio, established in the so-called Northern Province of Portuguese India, first in Tana and Baçaim and finally in Goa.  
The vessels would have been used to keep drinks cool and are part of a large and impressive set. Such vessels were known in the Middle Age, having become fashionable in various countries after being adopted by the court of Louis XIV.
677db211-c58d-50b1-b232-635d73f3327c.short_description: This pair of coolers with another pair with the same shape and decoration is unique both in type and shape among the export Chinese porcelain. They are part of a magnificent set that includes cutlery cases, sugar holders and special bottles with covers and trays. The like of this set has not been copied or produced in Chinese export porcelain for other Portuguese or foreign patrons.
677db211-c58d-50b1-b232-635d73f3327c.method_for_datation: According to prints of the medieval period it was common throughout Europe,namely around 1683, for large metallic basins with handles to be placed on the ground to hold bottles and ewers during mealtimes. In time these metal prototypes were sent to China by the Portuguese merchants, the East India companies from several European countries and from the USA, as well as by private merchants. Chinese potters copied these vessels in porcelain and decorated them according to clients’ taste.
677db211-c58d-50b1-b232-635d73f3327c.obtention: In 1911 both objects were transferred from the Convent of Santos-o-Novo to the Museu Nacional da Arte Antiga.

739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.name: Scene showing a squadron of Hussars
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.description: At the time of Count Kazimir Drašković (1716–1765) part of his *banderium* was barracked in Trakošćan. His military biography during the reign of Empress Maria Theresia still decorates the rooms and inventory of Trakošćan Castle. He began his service in the Austrian army in 1734, and fought on the battlefields of Europe. His courage was notable on both the Italian and German battlefields in the war of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) and in the Seven Years' War (1756–1763). In 1763, promoted to artillery general, he then became a commanding general in Transylvania. He was decorated with the highest military order of the Austrian Empire – the Commander Cross of Maria Theresia. There are many items from his time in Trakošćan Castle: portraits of army officers, family members, flags and other material, and particularly wall paintings in the military cabinet on the second floor. The room has canvas wall coverings that give a complete picture of Count Drašković’s military units in the mid-18th century. The large painting consists of 11 parts; the eight larger ones show the *banderium* on parade, composed of 821 people; and the three smaller ones show military symbols, cannon, lances, drums and flags. The paintings are realistic and show in detail the soldiers' uniforms, weapons and the distribution of the units and their parts. A schematic presentation, the soldiers have no personal characteristics, but are portrayed according to type with dark moustaches and red cheeks while the infantry units are faithfully rendered; the soldiers distributed in two companies of fusiliers and one of grenadiers. The staff includes hunters, musicians, guards and a canteen, a surgeon and NCOs. Especially interesting is the small band: the first painting of a military band in Croatia. This was the count's own professional band, which played at his castle during peacetime. It consisted of eight wind instrumentalists: four oboists, two fagottists and two horn players. It also had a tambour major. The cavalry has two squadrons of Dragons and three squadrons of Hussars. The scene shown here is the light cavalry of the Hussars, three troops placed one behind the other in two rows each. They are dressed in blue dolmans, red trousers, brown cloaks and light-brown boots. On their heads, they have busbies.
739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.short_description: In a landscape are three double rows of cavalry in blue uniforms led by officers mounted on white horses. There are several houses above the units. This scene, painted on canvas wall hangings, is part of a series depicting military units, which covered one of the rooms of Trakošćan Castle. Croatia's most important aristocratic family, the Counts Drašković, owned the castle. General Count Kazimir Drašković, from whose time these hangings date, had a distinguished military career and was decorated with the highest military order of the Austrian Empire – the Commander Cross of Maria Theresia.

739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.method_for_datation: Analysis of style and comparison with the Small Genealogy of the Drašković family.

739d0ddb-7438-5fa6-b2ce-791163929d75.obtention: The wall painting was made either to fit the wall of another room in Trakošćan Castle or some other building that belonged to the Counts Drašković, and was later adapted to fit the cabinet, probably when Trakošćan Castle was renovated in the second half of the 19th century.

73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.name: Sugar bowl
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.description:
The master, Domokos Kuny’s father, founded a pottery in Buda producing faience and ceramics in what is today Christina Boulevard. Three masters and eight apprentices worked in his manufactory in the 1780s. The products of the workshop were extremely popular among the bourgeoisie and aristocracy of Buda and Pest in the late 18th century.  
The white glazed sugar bowl is decorated with floral motifs and on the base is the sign “OF” (Ofen=Buda). Domokos Kuny’s (1754–1822) father was Dominique Cuny who mastered the craft of ceramics in a Strasbourg manufactory before arriving from Baden-Durlach to Holics in Upper Northern Hungary. The commercial and economic development of Buda attracted him and he settled down in the city in 1784–85 and founded a manufactory. In the surrounding countryside were clay mines, perfect for the production of ceramics.
73ac7a0b-2d07-5206-9603-0f364d1a8faa.short_description: An object of everyday use from the workshop of the famous master Domokos Kuny (1754–1822).

79b21411-a495-509f-bd1b-4acb4fa78729.name: *Portrait of a Negro*
79b21411-a495-509f-bd1b-4acb4fa78729.description: Morgado de Setúbal, a late 18th-century Portuguese “genre” painter, is quite original in his approach to portraying popular and picturesque scenes. His Portrait and still-life works stand out for their representations of various social types in Portuguese society, where his focus was mainly on the working classes. In this painting he depicts a black slave or servant who wears poorly conserved clothes and points at the viewer. The painting is typical of the artist's use of bold forms and earthy colours.
79b21411-a495-509f-bd1b-4acb4fa78729.short_description: This portrait of a black slave or servant is an example of Portuguese “genre painting”. In his portrayal of popular and picturesque scenes, Morgado de Setúbal allows the viewer to appreciate some late 18th-century Portuguese social types.

7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.name: *The Laboratories of the Istituto delle Scienze of Bologna*
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.alternate_name: *The Visit of Frederick Christian of Poland to the Istituto delle Scienze of Bologna*
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.description: The *Insignia degli Anziani Consoli*, housed in the Archivio di Stato, of Bologna, are documents on parchment commissioned every two months, from 1530 to 1796. These bound 16 volumes celebrate the eight Anziani Consoli and the Gonfaloniere di Giustizia, a group of ruling magistrates. From the end of the sixteenth-century the names of the magistrates were written flanked by their coats of arms and a depiction of a significant event that took place during the bimester of their charge. These manuscripts provide an extraordinary visual chronicle illustrating more than two centuries of the city's history with six pictures a year. This picture, refers to the last bimester of 1739, shows the inside of the Istituto delle Scienze of Bologna during the visit of prince Frederick Christian of Poland. The prince is sitting examining a fortress plan. In the background are visible from the left: the anatomy room, the school of the nude, and the Institute library. On the top is the coat of arms of the eight Anziani Consoli and in the middle, that of the Gonfaloniere di Giustizia.
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.short_description: This illumination shows the Istituto delle Scienze of Bologna during the visit of Prince Frederick Christian of Poland. In the middle of the scene, the prince is examining a fortress plan; in the background it is possible to see the rooms of the Istituto.
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.initial_owner: Anziani Consoli of the town of Bologna
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.method_for_datation: The date of the illumination (1739, last bimester), the subject depicted and the patronage (the Anziani Consoli of Bologna) are inscribed in the caption, below the picture.
7b6c2e8c-8a34-50a4-8b04-8c9aeafdbdd9.obtention: This illumination, like the whole series, has always been housed in the archive of the Bolognese senate, inside the municipal palace. It was transferred to the Archivio di Stato in 1874, when it was created.

7b88767b-c926-51da-aa90-991176a84ae4.name: City Hall Landsberg
7b88767b-c926-51da-aa90-991176a84ae4.description:
The City Hall, which is only 12 metres wide, housed on the ground floor the so-called “Brothaus” (a hall for selling bread), and in the basement, the jailhouse plus the communal wine cellar. Located on the upper floors are the two assembly halls of both chambers of the City Council, with the smaller room on the first floor used by the Inner Council, and the larger room on second floor used by the Outer Council. The third floor served the purpose of the ballroom.  
The façade of the City Hall is steeply proportioned and divided regularly into five vertical axes whose windows seem to grow from floor to floor, corresponding to the importance of the rooms behind them. A portal, flanked by columns, at one time accentuated the unadorned ground floor. Like a closely meshed web, a rich stucco decoration of Regency interlacing covers the flat surface of the facade, the integrated iconographic programme of which proclaims the respect the city's government will pay to the virtues, resulting in the success of the whole community. The higher floors are linked by narrow rearward-folded pilasters carried by putti, and united by a partially scrolled entablature over the third floor. “S”-shaped volutes are employed as consoles for the pilasters, but also as framework in which putti, as substitute carriers of the pilasters, alternate with vases and the three allegories of the virtues. The latter, in the form of heroic Old-Testament busts: Susanna and the Elders, Judith with the head of Holofernes, and presumably the Queen of Sheba, symbolise the constancy, bravery and wisdom of the city and its government. The theme is heightened on the second storey, with the display of five vertical oval-bust reliefs, showing antique heroes and generals as symbols of military power and prudence. Furthermore, the fully plastic figurative decoration in the gable area adds to this profane canon of virtues a religious level of meaning: at its centre there is a niche framed by pilasters in which personifications of Charity (*Caritas*) and Hope (*Spes*) hold the laurel wreath of victory above the city's coat-of-arms. By being depicted three-dimensionally, the cross of the latter also signifies ambiguously Faith (*Fides*), so that all three theological virtues are shown. Like a crown, a statue of Justice (*Justitia*) originally stood amidst the strutted gable, instead of the today's obelisk with the eye of the Lord at the top, as an absolutely necessary virtue of a promising government.
7b88767b-c926-51da-aa90-991176a84ae4.short_description: The City Hall of the Bavarian commercial town Landsberg am Lech flaunts a richly decorated façade, which is said to be a *magnum opus* of the famous plasterer Dominikus Zimmermann in this genre of profane architecture. He developed for this a system of order and decoration which combines elements of Italian architectural design with examples of French ornamental graphics that were popular at the time, and which covers the facade like a fine web. The allegory weaved-in implores a righteous municipal government leading to prosperity.

Stadt Landsberg a. Lech (ed.), *Das Landsberger Rathaus. Zur Wiedereröffnung des historischen Rathauses nach der Renovierung im Mai 1991* (Heimatgeschichtliches aus Landsberg am Lech 3), Landsberg am Lech 1991.  
Lampl, S., *Dominikus Zimmermann*, Munich 1987, pp. 274–79.  
Bauer, H. and A., *Johann Baptist und Dominikus Zimmermann. Entstehung und Vollendung des bayerischen Rokoko*, Regensburg 1985, pp. 18, 128–9, 299.
7b88767b-c926-51da-aa90-991176a84ae4.history: In the former Bavarian frontier town, one year after the old city hall was torn down in 1698 because of its ruinous state, a residential building located at the western area of the main square was renovated to become today’s City Hall, being located in the range of vision of the most important gate and therefore catching every visitor’s eye. In 1718, the building was heightened by a storey to incorporate a festivity hall and the scrolled gable of the facade. In the same year, Zimmermann and his workshop stuccoed the second storey vestibule and the assembly hall of the Outer Council; and in 1719, finally, the facade. Since then, a few restorations have taken place, some of which have led to alterations: in about 1800 the scrolled gable was simplified and also the portal by removal of its columns, and much later, between 1870 and1905, the upper halls were redecorated in the antique taste.

7e279011-a2bd-502b-84db-8a11eb8ed147.name: Liebert Palace
7e279011-a2bd-502b-84db-8a11eb8ed147.description: The shorter facade oriented towards the Maximiliansstrasse is, according to the role of the street in the cityscape, the most prominent and most visible side of the palace. There, the three-story building is structured with a small central projection which unites several stately elements, such as a broad archway, a balcony in the *piano nobile* and a gable with the coat-of-arms of von Liebenhofen. The building evokes a discreet splendour following the example of French Classicism. On the contrary, the long facade facing the Katharinengasse seems quite monotonous. The large ballroom (23 x 11 m) ranging over two storeys is the showpiece of the building. The rich decoration, executed entirely in the local “Augsburgian taste” Rococo style, was probably designed by Gregorio Guglielmi, who also painted the ceiling fresco. The walls are adorned with ornamentally framed panels (wood carving by Placidius Verhelst) partially filled with mirrors or paintings, as are the over-doors, which illustrate local and exotic flora and fauna. The stuccowork by the brothers Franz-Xaver and Simpert Feichtmayr is maybe the most superb element of the decoration. Especially the cornices of the upper windows, which freed from all architectural constraints, are an outstanding masterpiece. Their ornamental richness establishes a floating connection with the frame of the fresco. All in all, a masterly Rococo interior of courtly ambition.
7e279011-a2bd-502b-84db-8a11eb8ed147.short_description: The Schaezlerpalais, built for a rich banker, is the most important secular building in the city of Augsburg. Situated prominently in the centre of the city’s main street, its noble splendour coins the cityscape. The impressively lush interior decoration is an outstanding example of the local Rococo style, the so-called *Augsburger Geschmack* (Augsburgian taste). The ballroom in particular is especially large and ostentatious, even for a private palace.
7e279011-a2bd-502b-84db-8a11eb8ed147.method_for_datation: Documented in the archive; signature of the ceiling fresco, signed “1767”.

Hagen, B. Von, Wegener-Hüssen, A., *Stadt Augsburg* (Denkmäler in Bayern VII.83), Munich 1994, pp. 310–13.

7e279011-a2bd-502b-84db-8a11eb8ed147.history: The Augsburgian banker and silver-trader Benedict Adam Liebert von Liebenhofen (1730–1810) whose business connections were wide-reaching in international markets, commissioned the construction of the palace (1765–70 executed by local builder, Johann Gottfried Stumpe) in a prime location on the city’s main street. The occasion for the project was the ennoblement of Liebert to the rank of a Reichsritter (knight), which required an adequate, new and representative residence. For the design of his palace Liebert engaged internationally-renowned artists, as for instance, the courtly master-builder Karl Albert von Lespillez from Munich and the Roman mural painter Gregorio Guglielmi who, as a travelling artist, also worked for the imperial court in Vienna.

8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.name: Fireplace mirror
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.description:
A type of console mirror for use above a fireplace, it has imitation legs in the form of flat scrolls. The mirror itself is octagonal, a richly carved frame of ornate C- and S-scrolls and pierced *rocaille* surround it.  
Two unidentified coats-of-arms, incorporated into the scrollwork, extend into candle stands from which two angels' heads peep out from the crest formed by shell ornaments.  
The mirror furnished the Hütterott family mansion on Crveni otok island, near Rovinj in Istria. A German family of merchants and industrialists from Trieste, their presence in Rovinj began in 1890 when Johann Georg Hütterott opened a climatic health resort there and bought nearby islets, the family playing a major role in the overall advancement of the Rovinj area.
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.short_description: The carved gilded frame decorated in a characteristically mid-18th century style, with C- and S-scrolls and pierced *rocaille* belongs to a type of mirror for use above a fireplace. It came from the mansion of the Hütterott family on Crveni otok near Rovinj, which today is a hotel. The merchant and industrialist Hütterott family from Trieste bought several islets near Rovinj in 1890. They advanced the whole Rovinj area, and among other things laid out an exceptional park in Rovinj itself.
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.provenance: From the manor of the Hütterott family on Sv. Andrija island, which after 1945, was renamed Crveni otok island near Rovinj, Istria.
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.obtention: Transferred by way of the Commission for the Collection and Preservation of Cultural Monuments, Antiquities and Libraries KOMZA, formed in 1946.

8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.name: Villa Zanchini-Garagnani
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.description:
The villa is formed by the superimposition of eighteenth-century elements on the original nucleus of the building, once crowned by a small covered terrace (altana) on the top of the roof.  
The scenographic solution of the front with lateral arcades forms an aedicule that covers the curved stairs. This elegant feature was used as an entrance for coaches. The two hexagonal aedicules can be dated to the seventeenth-century and were attributed to the local architect Giovan Giacomo Monti. The curved flight of stairs is similar to solutions employed in Bolognese buildings of the same age, so that this part of the villa can be considered the first to be built.  
Distributed around the central hall are several different rooms. The elegant and measured interiors can be dated to the latest transformation that involved the building, at the end of the nineteenth-century. The rooms are decorated with stucco in Neo-classic style and in some case they still hold their original “Venetian style” floors.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.short_description:
The originality of this villa is the scenographic structure of its front formed by different arcades that hide and, at he same time, introduce to the two-curved stair flights, bringing to the first floor.  
The dynamism and elegance of the space and the changing views that can be enjoyed through the arcades and columns from the small loggia on the top of the stairs, are typical of the local baroque architecture that owns most of its devices to the theatre tradition.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.dates: 1679; 1786; 1881 restoration of the building and decoration of the interiors in Neo-classic style
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.bibliography: Matteucci, A. M.,*Ville storiche di Zola Predosa*, Province of Bologna, Municipality of Zola Predosa, without date.
8b0ad025-caaf-5480-92dd-b93f91fa88c5.history:
Not much is known about this villa and its architect remains unidentified. A Latin inscription, still visible on the building, tells us that it was built in 1679 by Edoardo Zanchini. At the beginning of the eighteenth-century the villa passed to the Zambeccari family and in 1786 it was restyled and enlarged by Marquis Vincenzo Zambeccari. In 1878 it was sold in a public auction to Raffaele Garagnani who promoted some restoration work and took the villa back to its original splendour.  
The whole building was seriously damaged during the Second World War. The private chapel next to the villa was destroyed and the roof was completely rebuilt by the Garagnani Family. They still own the villa and the surrounding land with vineyards and orchards.

8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.name: Console
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.description: From a base with four round feet springs the console resembling two vine branches, intertwined with vine-leaves and grapes. The carving is powerful as the volumes are full and in the round. The wood is gilded with silver leaf. The table is painted to look like a dark green false marble, with pale green veins. Formerly thought to be a nineteenth-century remake from a Tuscan workshop, today this console is considered an original piece dating to the eighteenth-century. The original provenance is unknown, but it was likely made in Tuscany. The console is part of the furniture of the baroque apartment, on the first floor of the building which was made between 1736 and 1738 for the wedding of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.short_description: This piece of furniture is very original; the base is made of vine-shoots and grapes realistically intertwined with a strongly naturalistic carving. We don’t know its original provenance. The console is housed in the red living room of the baroque apartment on the first floor of Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1736 and 1738 for the marriage of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.dates: First half of the eighteenth century

8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.name: *Portrait of Tommaso Campeggi and his Family*
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.description:
This painting formerly credited to the Lombard painter Pier Francesco Cittadini, has been recently reattributed to the Bolognese painter Lorenzo Pasinelli (1998). The portrait is characterised by the presence of such Nordic elements as the dark background and the analytical description of the 12 people. Pasinelli probably painted the great canvas during his stay in Rome, as a present for his host Tommaso Campeggi, the ambassador of Bologna to the Holy See. In 1666 it was moved to the palace owned by Tommaso Campeggi in via San Mamolo, in Bologna. When the house was sold the picture was moved to the residence of “Strà San Donato” and finally to the castle of Dozza, the Campeggi country residence.  
It is one of the rare examples of group portraits in Bolognese baroque painting. The impression is that of an austere and somewhat provincial aristocracy. They are not concerned with being carefully examined by the painter and only interested in portraiture for its social implications. The family is sitting in the traditional scheme, following a hierarchical order and rigidly divided in two groups, males and females. The first born is given central position, next to his sisters who are holding his gloves. Tommaso is the most static and affected figure with rigid authoritarianism, whilst the elegance of the clothes is more emphasized in the female figures.
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.short_description: The painting depicts the entire Campeggi family. The result is a perfectly balanced mixture of Bolognese and northern features combined with compositional and technical skill.
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.provenance: Casa Campeggi, via San Mamolo, Bologna
8ec0ecf7-b1a9-5b83-9f8a-0dc7cfe15831.obtention: Moved from Rome to the Campeggi residence of Bologna, later to the country residence of Dozza.

8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.name: Catholic Guild Church of St. Joseph
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.alternate_name: Church of the Brotherhood of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph for Craftsmen
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.description: The church is composed of two storeys. While the crypt is formed of two octagonal crypt chapels – a simplification of Herkomer’s plan for a holy sepulchre – the upper storey is composed of two simple quadratic spatial components for nave and choir. The centralised design is underlined by rounded corners. The powerfully built arcade-above-pilaster piers clearly divide the two sections, while reuniting the two in the overall prospect. Sweeping, erect proportions and bold accents lend the building qualities that clearly extend beyond that of a country chapel.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.short_description: St. Joseph’s in Bichlbach is the only surviving guild church in Austria. This is its primary significance, as opposed to its architectural and artistic qualities. The exterior of the church located on a hill above the village is plain, but however the interior of the centralised hall building with lightly slanted corners and adjoining choir, displays architectural ambition and charm. Here the spatial impression is completely dominated by the mighty high altar.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.method_for_datation: Founding charter of the guild from Emperor Leopold I with the plans from Herkomer, issued in 1694.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.bibliography: Dussler, H., *Der Allgäuer Barockbaumeister Johann Jakob Herkomer*, Kempten 1956, pp. 71–4.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.history: The origin of St. Joseph’s is directly connected to the social conditions in Außerfern. In summer there was virtually no work for the craftsmen who were thus forced to take to the road as journeymen. Church services, held on their departure and return, were celebrated together in the guild church. The brotherhood under the patronage of St. Joseph, the patron saint of craftsmen, was founded by the parish priest Lukas Egger in 1690 (certified by Emperor Leopold I in 1694). The founding charter already contained initial plans for the church building drawn up by Herkomer, master builder of Füssen, however their execution was delayed. The building was finally begun in 1710 according to new plans and was largely completed in the space of two years. The consecration did not take place until 1726.
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.patrons: Parish Priest Lukas Egger/Guild of Masons and Carpenters
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.architects: Architecture, first plan: Johann Jakob Herkomer (1652–1717); re-planning and construction work: Andreas Hafenegger (1666–1745); superstructure: Johann Georg Pauer [n.d.]; altar paintings, attributed to: Johannes Heel (1686–1749) or Paul Zeiller (1658–1738); crucifix: attributed to Andreas Thamasch (1639–1697)
8f662d2b-9ace-58c0-aaf7-2d20f5416ff7.author: Frank Purrmann

91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.name: Águas Livres Aqueduct
91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.description: The aqueduct has three main parts: the Mãe d'Água reservoirs located near the spring at the beginning of the course in the Carenque valley; the aqueduct and its secondary aqueducts spreading out around the city with a total length of 58.135 km. The system includes arches over the Alcântara valley. These are 941 m in length with an ensemble of 35 arches of which 14 are pointed and 21 are round. The ultimate destination of the Águas Livres aqueduct is the Mãe d'Água reservoir delivering water to the city. The reservoir is a wide, vaulted construction with an approximate capacity of 5,500 m3. The formal structure is perfectly justifiable for a work of this nature, which demands various materials and rational engineering. The incredible height of the rises of the Aqueduct's arches in the Alcântara valley is astonishing. The technical audacity is largely due to the Custódio Vieira's knowledge of engineering. The aqueduct pays homage to Roman models as it is imposingly “imperial” in its monumentality and even in its geographic position. The scarce ornamentation of Mãe d'Água das Amoreiras reservoir is compensated by the scale of the work and imposition of the vast stripped and solemn walls, as if the building was in fact a temple of the waters.
91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.short_description: An aqueduct using a classic system of gravity to capture, conduct and distribute water to the city of Lisbon. An open-air structure, it is mainly known for its monumental pointed arches over the Alcântara valley. There are also the underground galleries, the Mãe d'Água reservoir, and other springs dotted throughout its course. The main, oldest spring is located in the municipality of Sintra, which is endowed with adjacent works, canals and fountains.

91f210fe-567e-5899-a3c0-693a551d2636.history: At the beginning of João V's reign, the water supply in Lisbon was at a critically low state so in 1723, in an attempt to overcome the problem, Claudio do Amaral (attorney of west Lisbon) proposed that a study should be carried out on the spring at the Belas Águas Livres. He hoped that the study would allow water from the Belas Águas Livres to be channelled via an aqueduct into Lisbon. The king supported this decision and granted the means necessary to fund the aqueduct such as, in 1729, imposing a tax on the sale of certain goods entering the city (meat, wine, straw, olive oil and salt). Work began on the aqueduct in 1731 and, although construction didn't finish until approximately 1799, water was first channelled by the structure to Lisbon in 1744.

For the fountain: engineer, Miguel Ângelo Blasco (active 1769–1770); architect: Reinaldo Manuel dos Santos [n.d.].

92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.name: Palazzo Poggi’s Observatory
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.description:
Built to easily view the entire night sky, the Observatory has an elevated and massive structure and is shaped like a tower. The upper part is located over a large terrace which is jutting out. On top, stands a large chamber with wide windows, rotated 90˚ from the axis of the tower below.  
It is known that the Observatory was modified by the architects with the help of many experts including learned scientists working at the Institute, such as Eustachio Manfredi.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.short_description: Together with the anatomical theatre in the Palace of the Archiginnasio, the Observatory is the most important evidence of Bolognese scientific culture and activity during baroque age. Both were connected with places of learning: while the first was part of the so-called ‘studio’, the famous, local University, the second was created as part of the Eighteenth century Institute of Sciences and Arts, a very modern institution where, according with the project of the founder, the count and general Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, scientists and artists should have collaborated in researching and teaching.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.bibliography:
Matteucci, A. M., *Carlo Francesco Dotti e l'architettura bolognese del Settecento*, Bologna, 1969, pp. 100-101.  
Lenzi, D., “Le trasformazioni settecentesche”, *Palazzo Poggi: da dimora aristocratica a sede dell'Università di Bologna* (ed. A. Ottani Cavina), Bologna, 1988, pp. 58-78.
92585462-61ce-5c52-97cd-a33e4c532b42.history: The Observatory was created as part of the Institute of Sciences and Arts. The Institute, due to the farsighted outlook of its founder, Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, was composed of two academies. The first was devoted to scientific studies, while the second was intended for the teaching of the arts. At the beginning of the eighteenth century it became necessary to find an appropriate building to house the Institute. Among the requirements for a suitable building was the stability of the structure in order to erect an Observatory on the roof. The Academy purchased the sixteenth century palace owned by the cardinal Giovanni Poggi. The Observatory was started in 1712 under the direction of the architect Giovanni Battista Torri. After his death, the following year, Carlo Francesco Dotti, architect of the Observatory, modified the plan. The work was finished in 1725.

938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.name: *Remembrance*
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.description:
A young woman in a coat lined with fur gazes out of the picture lost in thought while knitting a stocking and no longer listening to the sound of a violin. It appears that the music has reminded her of a past situation probably of a romantic nature. The violinist, sensing the woman's mental absence, remains in the background. A richly decorated mirror, glossy box, knitting basket, a broken string of pearls and precious sheet in the right-hand corner, make up a sentimental still life. The emotional air of the picture is accentuated by a landscape on the wall of an otherwise austere interior.  
Genre painting was once considered low and its subjects trivial if picturesque and amusing. With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the actions and relationships between people, originating in 17th century Dutch burgher culture, became increasingly important. Pictures typically combined landscape, genre painting and narrative, with conversation often providing a vehicle for the “action”. Conversation scenes between men and women were particularly popular. They were largely based on the Dutch “fine style” promoted by Rembrandt's student Gérard Dou in Leyden, and shaped by the Scandinavian tradition of attention to detail and close observation of reality. While Rembrandt arrived at expressive internal visions, painters of the Leyden school mastered the techniques of representing different materials – later taken up by the Biedermeier. Pictures by the “*Fijnschilders*” were highly valued and sought after in their time. The word *fijn* encompasses more than the obvious notion of something fine, holding connotations including nice, refined, elegant, apt, precise and sensitive. In 18th-century Central Europe the style found admirers among both art collectors and painters. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters Frans van Mieris and Dou into pleasant pictures. He was also a competent portraitist, restorer and art dealer.
938149f6-52f2-528c-8af6-89d9c8a0c702.short_description: With the escalating social whirl of the 18th century the subject of the relationships between people, originating in 17th-century Dutch burgher culture, became important. Braun, a member of the Vienna Academy, often transformed moralist paintings by the Dutch painters F. Mieris and G. Doue into pleasant pictures.

97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.name: *Portrait of the Beneficiary Faustino das Neves*
97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.description:
Strongly influenced by her father, Baltazar Gomes Figueira, and by painters such as Francisco Zurbarán, Juan de Roelas and Daniel Seghers, Josefa de Ayala worked in a small provincial centre outside Lisbon. Away from the court, and in a place where the medieval lifestyle was preserved, she related to the politics opposed to the Spanish Habsburg dynasty, supporting the Restoration cause of the Royal House of Braganza. The social life of this micro-society revolved around social gatherings and meetings in convents and noble residences. The noblemen – members of the Municipal Senate – religious orders, brotherhood and charitable institutions with whom she fraternized, were well-read and had no economic restrictions. In their homes were many works of art some of which were commissioned from local provincial artists.  
From as early as the 17th century, Josefa had several biographies written about her. Costa Meesen (1696) referred to her “cleanliness and aptitude” upon imitating “things from nature”. Writer Damião Froes Perym (1736) also praises her “skill, beauty, honesty and charm” and her moral virtues. In the 19th century, José Silvestre Seabra and Almeida Garrett made reference to *Portrait of the Beneficiary Faustino das Neves*, considering it the genre which best revealed the sensitive side of Josefa d'Óbidos. The piece got lost in time and in 1957 it was identified by Reis-Santos as the work of Josefa d'Óbidos.  
The artist perfectly captures the psychology of this distinguished man from Óbidos. His dark clothing and his vigorous look contrast with the luminosity of the white and beige of his face, accentuating the Counter-Reformation features of the piece. The male figure, accompanied by an angel announcing his death, is purposely decentralised relative to the axis of the composition. This is a peculiarity which enhances the formal skills of Josefa de Ayala thus allowing her to be included within the ranks of the best 17th-century Portuguese painters.
97284ed3-c2ab-51af-8cd2-2ae8ea41f09e.short_description: Josefa de Ayala skilfully conveys the psychology through the glance, gesture and pose of this distinguished man from the town of Óbidos. His dark clothing and vigorous look contrast with the luminosity provided by the white and beige tones of his face. The figure is accompanied by an angel announcing his death.

982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.name: Monument to Luigi Ferdinando Marsili
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.description: This monument was commissioned by the Institute of Sciences of Bologna to commemorate one of its main founders, General Luigi Ferdinando Marsili in 1733, three years after his death. The monument is located in the right arm of the transept of the church of St. Dominic in Bologna which was refurbished a few years before by the architect Dotti. It is made of a very poor material, stucco, which is a mixture of marble powder and sand. Many Bolognese sculptors used stucco in the Baroque age to create true masterpieces for churches and noble residences. From the church wall hangs a great and rich curtain covering objects once beloved by the General; books, weapons, and artist tools. The upper portion is occupied by the slender figure of Fame, holding in her hand a trumpet and an oval medallion with Marsili’s profile. Under the diagonally projecting slab with its Latin inscription struggles Time, represented as an old man with a sickle. The baroque theme of Fame defeating Time is perfectly conveyed.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.short_description: This monument represents the baroque spirit in the use of allegories, in the employment of many diagonals crossing in the composition and in the dynamic movement transmitted to the sculpted curtain.
982741b5-3e8b-59ac-988e-567fb8f0a6fa.method_for_datation: The monument date is established thanks to archive documents and to the Latin inscription.

986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.name: *St. Florian with a View of Jihlava*
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.description:
The picture is a typical example of a votive painting designed for a town environment. In their everyday prayers and pledges, people of the period turned to saints as protectors against the various perils of life. The promotion of saints in these roles was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, was among the most worshipped. Here the saint is depicted as the protector of the town of Jihlava. Under Swedish siege during the Thirty Years' War the town suburbs were burnt down and the majority of the houses were destroyed. Only one-eighth of the Jihlava population survived.  
Jihlava is the oldest mining town of the Czech lands, renowned in the Middle Ages for its silver mines. Mining law was codified there for the first time in Central Europe, alongside municipal law. This formulary law became a template for a number of other mining towns. The economic development of Jihlava was facilitated by trade and crafts, especially weaving. In the mid-18th century, Jihlava was the second largest manufacturer of cloth in the Habsburg monarchy. This *veduta* is dominated by the Jesuit Church of St. Ignatius, with the parish Church of St. James in the background, on the right; the whole town is encircled by its walls. The square is lined with stone buildings, with arcades and a town hall that feature different types of vaulting. The regular ground plan of the right-angled network of streets with a square in the centre, the largest in Moravia, was defined by a building order made by King Přemysl Otakar II in 1270.  
The work of Václav Nosek has not yet been fully mapped as it has a relatively broad span. After settling in Jihlava in 1702, he worked for the town as well as for the Bishop of Olomouc (Kroměříž, 1711) and the Premonstratensian monastery in Louka u Znojma (*Education of the Virgin Mary*, side altar, 1712). In the 1720s, Nosek also produced templates for graphic illustrations of Episcopal prints.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.short_description: The picture is a typical example of a votive painting. The promotion of saints as protectors was among the chief tools of re-Catholicisation in rural areas. St. Florian, protector from fire, is represented here as the patron saint of Jihlava, one of the largest and wealthiest Moravian towns.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.initial_owner: Parish Church of St. James, Jihlava
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.method_for_datation: The archivist and historian Johann Peter Cerroni states that Nosek painted a picture of St. Florian with a *veduta* of Jihlava. By stylistic comparison the work may be associated with the painting in the Moravian Gallery.
986dd8ef-8d48-564e-8d94-efc86002986d.obtention: The painting from the Highlands Museum, Jihlava was transferred to the Moravian Gallery in Brno in 1962. It probably comes from the parish Church of St. James.

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.name: *Paulines at Prayer*
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.description:
Their hands clasped in prayer, the Pauline brothers kneel on a paved balustraded terrace in a garden in front of a row of vases on pedestals with flowers in them, with palm trees behind them arranged in shortened perspective. The perspective of the composition, based on two intersecting linear scenes, shows the vision of the patron of the Paulines and St Paul the Hermit in a cave on the lawn. The vision of the Patron of the Paulines depicts the Virgin Mary, St. John the Baptist and the *Agnus Dei* with His leg curved around a flag with a cross.  
The use of perspective, accentuated by the row of classical pedestals, evokes an earlier style. The foreshortening decreases the depth of the scene and emphasises the initial pair of brothers and the first pedestal, which brings them closer to the front of the painting. The morphology and typology of the Pauline brother figures, St Paul the Hermit and the ornamental motifs on the vases together with the flowers in them, suggest a date of around 1740, being elements of the Baroque style. The work is in the style of the lay brother and painter, Ivan Ranger. Ranger, regarded as one of Croatia's greatest Baroque painters is most famous for his frescoes, which he painted in enormous numbers. Ranger was already a trained artist when he arrived at the Lepoglava monastery from Tyrol. The Pauline Order accommodated a number of lay brothers in their monasteries, comprising painters, sculptors, cabinet-makers and other masters of the arts and crafts. They produced works for the interiors of churches and monasteries in the monastery workshops.  
Lepoglava was the largest and most important Pauline monastery in Croatia. It was the main centre for educational and cultural learning, with a Latin grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. The Paulines, together with the Jesuits, played a key role in promoting Baroque art and culture in Croatia.
9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.short_description: The altarpiece, depicting the Pauline brothers in a garden praying in front of flower vases, is probably the work of the lay brother and painter Ivan Ranger, a trained artist who came from Tyrol. Ranger – who joined the Pauline Order in Lepoglava and remained there until he died – is regarded as one of Croatia’s greatest Baroque painters. He is especially famous for his frescoes, which decorate many Pauline interiors as well as other churches and monasteries. The Lepoglava monastery was the main centre of the Pauline Order. It had a grammar school and was the first Academy awarded the right to confer doctorates. Together with the Jesuits, the Paulines played a key role in advancing Baroque art and culture in Croatia.

9c3f798c-5e8a-5a8a-b7a4-72ba45140b9d.obtention: The Diocesan Museum in Zagreb was founded in 1939 to safe-keep church artworks that for various reasons were in danger of devastation. This altarpiece was placed in the museum to preserve it.

9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.name: Sunflowers frame
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.description:
From an inventory of the properties of Vincenzo Bargellini, these pendant frames made in 1750 were originally made for holding mirrors, today they hold pictures. They were shown at an exhibition in Bologna in 1935 on Bolognese eighteenth-century art. At that time the frame was still holding a mirror.  
No mention is made of these frames in Vincenzo Bargellini's letters to Venice to commission furniture. Therefore, it is believed they were made in Bologna by local craftsmen following Roman and Venetian models.  
The high quality of the work is evident in the rich and naturalistic decoration. The sunflowers are an allusion to a particular destination.  
A frame similar to this pair is held in the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna; the evolution of this same style can be recognised in the frames made for the pictures by Marcantonio Franceschini exhibited in this same museum, made especially for the paintings in 1710–1711.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.short_description:
The extraordinary vivacity of this mirror frame testifies at a very early stage (1699) the great skill and the refined taste of Bolognese baroque carvers, who were looking at Rome and Venice for up to date ideas.  
The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects or documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.holder: Museo di Arte Industriale e Galleria Davia Bargellini
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.method_for_datation: The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects of documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to that of one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.obtention: This frame together with its pendant is mentioned in the 1750 inventory of Vincenzo Bargellini, at that time it was holding a mirror. It is exhibited in the museum since 1924, after the convention between the Municipality of Bologna and the Opera pia Davia Bargellini (owner of the picture gallery and of some of the family furniture).

9dd60e86-bef2-5b84-bc64-d726595a61b1.name: Armillary sphere from the Grammar School, Varaždin
9dd60e86-bef2-5b84-bc64-d726595a61b1.description:
An armillary sphere used as an astrological instrument to teach the distances between planets and stars and to measure time in the Jesuit Grammar School in Varaždin. Engraved on the ring of the sphere are the signs of the Zodiac.  
The grammar school, founded by the Jesuit order in 1636, continued under the headship of the order until 1773 when Pope Clement XIV extinguished the order with his Bull of Suppression. The curriculum at the school was according to the Jesuit system and teaching was in Latin. Immediately after the suppression of the Jesuits, by decree of Empress Maria Theresia the Bishop of Zagreb, Josip Galjuf, took over the grammar school in Varaždin and other schools in Croatia and Slavonia. He appointed Anton Rajšp, former Jesuit and doctor of theology, as head of the grammar school. The Pauline order took over the school in 1776 but after suppression of the order by decree of Emperor Joseph II, Anton Rajšp became the head of the school again.

9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.name: Ship’s commode/oratory
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.description:
Oratories commonly belonged within a domestic context but an oratory desk was used either as a portable piece of furniture for religious purposes or as a cabinet-on-a-stand for reading. This particular oratory was used on board a ship and is the result of a cumulative commercial exchange among merchants who travelled via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and ports or to north or north-western Europe. This is why it is probable that the ship's commode would have been influenced by several artistic styles: from Coromandel (the south-eastern coast of the Indian Peninsula), Chinese folding screens (*Henan*), or English Japanned furniture.  
Designed by Gaspar Ferreira and Manuel Silva, the commode was built to enable sailors and passengers to practice their religious routines on board ship. Probably commissioned by King D. João V, it is composed of two parts: the inferior part consists of three drawers and a desk with an oblique lid; while the superior section is shaped like a cupboard with a gabled segmental arch topped by the royal coat of arms.  
Carved and sculpted urns with flares decorate the top edges. Painted in bright red lacquer it has black decorative tablets and gilded iconographic motifs or *chinoiseries* – Chinese scenes. Both the design and ornamentation are characteristic of the so-called D. João V style. On the inside of the cupboard is an oratory with the following figures: St. Anthony of Lisbon on the right and St. Barbara on the left flanking Christ Crucified. The inside of the doors are painted with scenes of the Passion of Christ (Christ with the Cross; Lord of Cana Verde on the right; Christ tied to the Column and the Resurrection of Christ on the left).
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.short_description: A large commode/oratory with a cupboard, for use on board ship. The black decorative tablets are decorated with vegetal elements, while Chinese scenery – known as *chinoiserie* – decorates the larger panels.
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.dimensions: H: 268 cm; w: 72 cm; width: 44 cm
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.obtention: Deposited at the museum by the Pinto Basto Family, founder of the Vista Alegre factory in the 19th century

a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.name: Vojković Palace
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.description: The Late Baroque palace occupied the sites of three older plots. Although the remains of the older houses bring about certain irregularities, the architect created a well-worked out spatial organisation within the framework of the three-winged, U-shaped ground plan. The covered passageway or entrance on the ground floor, and the hall that surmounts it in the same format on the top floor, placed the whole length of the entrance wing on the central axis, giving the building its particular quality. Two symmetrical stairways ascend to small vestibules either side of the entrance to the hall. The fact that here, unlike contemporary Croatian palaces, the characteristic passageway along the courtyard façade was omitted, the double sequences of rooms along the side-wings compensate for this anomaly. The palace achieves equal architectural value exteriorly. The central entranceway passage and hall on the façade are emphasised by their projections, and what is more, the hall achieves independence in the roof area too, emphasised by a scalloped, contoured gable. The elements of articulation, particularly on the window frames and the pilasters, are characterised by the plasticity and dynamics of the Late Baroque, and their enhanced grouping on the central projection – accented by the portal of the undulating gable – is in line with the entire architectural concept of the palace. In this context, an important part is played by the urban location of the palace, which has an entrance façade facing the street that leads to the main square of the Upper Town (that of St. Mark ), while it is also located at the city's edge so that it includes a spacious garden. Thus, the palace contributes to the Baroque opening up of medieval fortified cities and characterises the Baroque synthesis of urban and out-of-town residences and distinctive garden palaces.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.short_description: The Late Baroque Vojković Palace in Zagreb's Upper Town is characterised by a well-worked-out organisation of space and volume that can be described as one of the most opulent aristocratic residences of the time in inland Croatia. The characteristic Baroque three-wing ground plan is organised around a central axis, with an entrance passageway on the ground floor and a hall on the first floor. Particular architectural prominence is given to the hall externally with an intricate gable projection. When the surrounding parkland is included, the building presents a typically Baroque unification of city- and country-house, known as a garden palace.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.type: Secular, three-winged palace with a central hall
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents and stylistic features.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.bibliography:
Horvat, A., (ed) “Barok u kontinentalnoj Hrvatskoj” in *Barok u Hrvatskoj*, Zagreb, 1982, pp. 1–381.  
Dobronić, L., *Palača Hrvatskog povijesnog muzeja 1764–2004*, Zagreb, 2004.
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.history: The Lieutenant Colonel of the cavalry troop at Banska Krajina (Border), Sigismund Volković, commissioned the palace in 1764. The Volković residence was the meeting place of the Zagreb elite and the venue for theatrical performances and concerts, particularly after the fire in Varaždin in 1776 when the *ban* (viceroy's) government returned to Zagreb's Upper Town and the nobility followed suit. Although the owner twice tried to sell the palace to the Zagreb County in the 19th century, the palace changed noble owners several times – the Oršićes, the Kulmers and finally the Rauch family. Today the palace houses the Croatian History Museum.
keywords: Zagreb, Vojković Palace, Late Baroque, three-winged ground plan, façade projection with prominent gable
a040baa1-05f4-547e-9513-6062cf60a5fb.author: Katarina Horvat-Levaj

a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.name: Holy Trinity Column, Olomouc
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.description: The column, on a hexagonal ground plan, is 35 m tall and has a chapel on the ground floor. It celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The sculpted decoration of the column consists of 12 sandstone statues of light-bearers, 12 reliefs with half-figures of the apostles, reliefs with allegories of Faith, Hope and Charity, a sculpture of the Assumption in the central part and, topmost, a sculpture of the Holy Trinity. There are 18 figures of the saints, including the patron saints of the country, preachers (John Capistranus was active in Olomouc) and martyrs. The Jesuit saint, Aloysius Gonzaga, was canonised at the time of the column’s construction (1726). Apart from gilding, the column was originally decorated with white marble.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.short_description: The column presents the largest grouping of Baroque statues within a single sculpture in Central Europe. In 2000 it was listed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site. The column celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The top sculpture of Christ the Saviour and God the Father, the ruler of the world, opens with Archangel Michael, symbol of the eternal struggle with heresy. The work, by several Olomouc masters, is one of the last memorial columns to be built under the Habsburg monarchy in several towns from the second half of the 17th century onwards.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.method_for_datation: The construction of the column is recorded in Town Council minutes; contracts with individual craftsmen have also been preserved.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.bibliography:
Pavel Zatloukal (ed), *Horní náměstí v Olomouci*, Olomouc, 1995.  
Miloš Stehlík, Slohová podstata sochařského díla Ondřeje Zahnera, *Opuscula Historiae Artium*, F 42, 1998, pp. 7–26.  
Marek Perůtka (ed), *Sloup Nejsvětější Trojice v Olomouci*, Olomouc, 2001.  
Miloš Stehlík, in Lubomír Slavíček (ed), *Josef Winterhalder d. J. (1743 Vöhrenbach – 1807 Znojmo). Maulbertschs bester Schüler*, Langenargen–Brno, 2009.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.history: The Holy Trinity Column was built as a counterpart to the Plague Column of the Virgin Mary in an adjacent square on the initiative of V. Render, a local master stonemason. He oversaw the construction and also contributed preliminary finance. Before his death in 1733, Render built the first-floor chapel. The invasion of the Prussian army in 1741 delayed the construction for which several local masters had joined forces. F. Sattler was responsible for some of the sculpted decoration of the column, with the larger part executed by O. Zahner. It is one of the last memorial columns to be built under the Habsburg monarchy in several towns from the second half of the 17th century onwards. Consecration of the column by the Bishop of Olomouc and Cardinal Troyer was conducted in the presence of Empress Maria Theresa and her husband František I of Lorraine. In 2000 the column was listed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site.
a1c80f71-d7bf-5009-be59-e7b7810ccda4.architects: Václav Render (1669–1733, Olomouc), Filip Sattler (1695 Wenns, Tyrol – 1738 Olomouc), Ondřej Zahner (1709 Ettershausen – 1752 Olomouc), Jan Šimon Forstner (1714? Salzburg – 1773 Olomouc), Wolfgang Träger (1714 Pilsen – 1763 Olomouc), Jan Michael Scherhauf (1724 Wels – 1792 Olomouc)

aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.name: Hellenbach Manor
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.description: Hellenbach Manor, known as the Marija Bistrica Castle, lies northwest of Marija Bistrica a famous shrine and place of pilgrimage dedicated to St. Mary. Built on a square plan, it has a central hall that is much higher than all the other rooms. The ground floor, the so-called *piano nobile*, is subordinate to the first floor. On the front façade, the porch is disposed of elegant Classical features: four columns connected by a baluster fence, which carries the high architrave and the triangular gable. A prominent central section defines the opposite façade. The first-floor rooms are elegantly decorated with stucco decoration in the Classical vocabulary of garlands, festoons, architraves and pilasters.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.short_description: The last quarter of the 18th century in northern Croatia was marked by the powerful influence of Classicism, with manors in the Classical style built parallel to residencies of the late Baroque. One of these was so-called Hellenbach Manor in Marija Bistrica. Built before 1786 by the Sermage family, in the 19th century the Hellenbach family purchased it. Hellenbach Manor is in the International Classical style inspired by a renewed interest in Palladianism, which spread from France in around 1750, and which other European cultural centres embraced.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.bibliography: Žmegač, A., “Dvorac Marija Bistrica” in *The Art topography of Krapinsko-zagorska County*, Zagreb, 2008, pp. 454–455.
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.history: Hellenbach Manor, probably built by the noble family Sermage, came into the possession of the Keglević family and then the Jelačić family. Finally, in 1851, the Hellenbach family purchased it.
keywords: Manor, domestic architecture, Classical architecture
aba7996a-fd1e-5045-baaa-28186fd15f15.author: Mirjana Repanić-Braun

ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.name: *The Illustrious Men of Budrio*
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.description: These paintings are good examples of the fashion of collecting and cataloguing local memories in a sort of Filopatria (love for one's home-town). This was typical of the baroque age and of the age of the Enlightenment. They are composed of several roundels that had to be filled from time to time with portraits of illustrious citizens. In the first painting are depicted doctors, soldiers, ecclesiastics and venerable men living between the Middle Ages and the Early Counter-reformation. Among them are Mercatello, a medical doctor in Bologna, Antonio Cossa, professor of Law, and Bartolomeo Garganelli, professor of Law and Astronomy. In the second painting, finished in 1799, we find especially ecclesiastics, diplomats and magistrates, philosophers, scientists, medical doctors and theologians: Francesco Muratori, professor of Anatomy, Vincenzo Menghini medical doctor and chemist, the local historian Domenico Golinelli and his son Ludovico, a clergy man; artists such as the follower of the Carracci Giacomo Lippi, the baroque painter Giovanni Battista Caccioli, the set designer Vincenzo Gotti; the architects Alfonso Torreggiani and Giuseppe Tubertini. In the third picture illustrious men not included in the first two are depicted, who were born before the end of the century, like the landscape painter Alberto Melonari, the “quadraturista” Giuseppe Carlo Gotti, the set designer and member of the Bolognese Accademia Clementina Alessandro della Nave, the illustrious chemist and pharmacist, Francesco Maria Coli, professor of the University of Bologna, Domenico Inzaghi and Don Giuseppe Benedetti from whose bequests to the town of Budrio were created the public library and the Pinacoteca.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.short_description: These paintings, hanging in the first room of the Pinacoteca, celebrate men born in Budrio who became famous in various fields including literature, politics, sciences and arts. Many of them are also part of the history of Bologna and its institutions because, given that they were born in Budrio, they are also Citizens of Bologna.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis; the tradition attributes them to the local painter Faustino Trebbi, for stylistic reasons it is thought he only painted the third one. The other two are probably the work of different artists.
ace50751-44b2-507a-97c4-64edc5800962.obtention: Public Library, then moved to the Pinacoteca (1989).
