ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.name: Book Cover
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.description:
A Baroque book cover of embossed silver and richly decorated with volutes, shells and acanthus foliage. Both the front and back covers have a central crest of two important families: the Crest of the Gaos (Gaus?) family of Rijeka on the front, and the crest of the Brajković family of Senj on the back. Mentioned initially in Rijeka in 1614, The Gaos (Gaus?) family appear in a document of 1616, as “de Hahnberg”. The Brajkovićs of Senj are a prominent Croatian family, descendants of the Miroslavić family, first mentioned in Poljica in 1420. One of the best-known members of the family was Martin Brajković (Senj 1668–Vienna 1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš from 1700 to 1703, and Bishop of Zagreb from 1703 until his death in 1708. Who ordered this book cover and why is unknown; similarly how these two families are connected in the first half of 18th century is also an unknown.  
There are two silver hallmarks on the object: one is a Venetian hallmark with St. Marcus, and the other is the control mark of Venetian mint “Zecca” that belongs to Zuanne Premuda who worked at assay control from 1712 to 1749.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.short_description: A Baroque book cover of embossed silver richly decorated with volutes, shells and acanthus foliage. The Crest of the Gaos (Gaus?) family of Rijeka is on the front, and the crest of the Brajković family of Senj on the back. One of the best-known members of the Brajković family was Martin Brajković (1668–1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš, and later Bishop of Zagreb.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.initial_owner: Gaus (Gaos?) family of Rijeka, or the Brajković family of Senj

ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.method_for_datation: The date and origin of the object are according to the hallmarks.
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.obtention: Donated by Draga Butković, Gundulićeva 22a, Zagreb, in 1957.

ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.name: Biblioteca Joanina da Universidade de Coimbra
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.description:
Outside, the royal coat of arms crowns the Baroque doorway as a memento of royal patronage. Inside, two identical triumphal arches link the three rooms and create a multiplicity of images that attract the eye to King João V's portrait overlooking the Library like an altar in a church.  
Competing with the Golden Libraries of central Europe, the *chinoiserie* motifs on the bookshelves, give the visitor a taste of exoticism, while the allegorical *trompe l'oeil* ceiling paintings recall Portuguese participation in globalisation.  
In this “noble” floor open to visitors, the shelves contain 28,943 books, but two more levels of shelving are in use today below this one where around 30,000 rare and antique books are stored.
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.short_description:
The Library of the University of Coimbra is an important example of civil Baroque architecture during the reign of King João V, and one of the most beautiful libraries in Europe. The main façade, with its four huge monolithic columns and arches connecting three spacious interior rooms, underline the notion that these are *royal* entrances to knowledge stored away in the library bookcases that cover the walls.  
On the wall facing the door is a portrait of King João V by the royal painter G. D. Duprà. The allegorical *trompe l'oeil* ceiling paintings by Simões Ribeiro (1723) create the illusion of the library being larger than it really is.
ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.bibliography:
Raczinski, Le Comte A., *Les Arts au Portugal, lettres adréssées à la Société artistique et Scientifique de Berlin (...)*, Paris, 1846.  
Pimentel, A. F., "O gosto oriental na obra das estantes da Livraria da Universidade de Coimbra", *IV Simpósio Luso-espanhol de História da Arte*, Coimbra, 1987.

ada03f89-9e12-51a6-b251-a9bcbfe3a40c.history: In 1716 the rector of the university requested of King João V some simple improvements to the university library in order to store new books on theology, philosophy and law acquired with the University’s new curricula. The King, however, saw this as an opportunity to aim higher and gave the university permission to construct a new, modern library.

adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.name: Palazzo Barberini (National Museum of Archaeology)
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.description:
The palace is characterised by the coexistence of ancient structures - the concave dual-ring terminal portico of the sanctuary whose column bases can be seen on the floor at the entrance - and the structures built between the late middle ages and the time of the Barberini tenure. The inscription of the main portal, dated 1498, and the coat of the arms of the Colonna family on the well are evidence of the significant work commissioned by the Colonna family. Two central flights of stairs in the *cavea* and the installation of the well give the palace the character of an urban development, enhanced by the axiality of the entire complex, and underlined by the fusion between the ancient and modern structures.  
The Barberini family (Taddeo and his son Maffeo) highlighted the penetration with antiquity scenically through the internal restructuring of the central hall, by the inclusion of the covered roof terrace to the front, and the addition of a cruciform *nymphaeum* to the rear (designed by Francesco Contini in 1660), as if intending to display symbolically – in a sort of ideal appropriation of antique and Roman history – the new status acquired by the family.  
This continuous dialogue with "reused" antiquity was further accentuated by some of the outstanding objects from the region that were housed within the palace by Taddeo's brother Cardinal Francesco Barberini (1597–1679). Most notable among these is the famous multicoloured mosaic of a Nile scene that was originally the floor of a basin, which was found in the apse-room of the lower temple. It remains one of the most interesting and peculiar items in the museum.  
The interior of the palace is richly decorated with frescos of mythological, biblical and historical scenes that are attributed to artists from Zuccari's circle and which date, therefore, to between the late 16th and first-half of the 17th century. The final urban development, undertaken by Maffeo Barberini in 1656, was the introduction of a road connecting the lower and upper sanctuaries, the palace and the church.
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.short_description: The palace is characterised by the coexistence of ancient structures of the 2nd-century BC Roman sanctuary and structures built on top of them between the late middle ages and the time of the Barberini family's tenure. It was this link with antiquity and Roman history that the Barberini family highlighted in their scenically penetrative plan for the palace, which was intended to display symbolically the new status acquired by the family, by means of a sort of ideal appropriation of antiquity and Roman history.
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.bibliography:
Romanelli, P., *Palestrina*, Naples 1967, pp. 83–86.  
Masella, L. and Fornari, Z., “L’attività architettonica …” in *I Barberini a Palestrina* (P. Tomassi ed.), Palestrina 1992, pp. 59–126.  
Barberini, F., “La famiglia Barberini” in *I Barberini a Palestrina* (P. Tomassi ed.), Palestrina 1992, pp. 7–36.  
*Il Museo archeologico di Palestrina* (S. Gatti ed.), Rome 1996.  
Baiocchi, G., “Palazzo/Museo Barberini”, *I Principi della Chiesa*, Milan 1998, pp. 174–175.
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.history: The town and Palace of Palestrina had been owned by the ancient feudal family of Prince Francesco Colonna until it was acquired by Pope Urban VIII (1623–44) in 1630 as a gift for his brother Carlo Barberini. The Barberinis, originally from Barberino in Val d’Elsa, were based initially in Florence where they were landowners and then merchants. In the 16th century the first prelate, Francesco (1528–1600) moved to Rome, and it was Taddeo Barberini, son of Carlo who died in 1630, who was responsible for the reorganisation and elevation of the palace. The palace crowns the slopes where a 2nd-century BC sanctuary dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia – famous in antiquity for her oracles – once stood. Having suffered bomb damage during the last war, in 1956, some ancient structures were revealed beneath the palace, which was then given to the State and turned into the National Museum of Archaeology.
adb7d372-346f-5c61-a66b-6041c7d412d5.patrons: Taddeo Barberini (1603, Rome – 1647, Paris), Prefect of Rome, and his son Maffeo (1630–85), from his marriage to Anna Colonna
keywords: Feudal palace, scenic, antiquity, Baroque, archaeology, museum, *nymphaeum*, water theatre

af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.name: Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.description:
The three-axis facade of the 18th-century, L-shaped, two-level, saddle-back-roofed building of the Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum is in the Classical style. The ground floor is adorned with simple toothing and the upper floor is embellished with surface decoration. The upper-floor windows have curved top-planes. The door frame of the former pharmacy entrance (in the middle axis of the street facade), and the red limestone frames of the windows on the ground floor, are adorned with carved garlands.  
Inside, the pharmacy service area was in the arched, divided space on the ground floor. Four pieces of oak furniture made by Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop are still in situ, including a carved and gilded unit with shelves of different lengths and widths, a worktop, cupboards and drawers; the names of medicines are written in Latin in white letters on the white surface of the cabinet drawers, which have handles of either brass or wood. The Empire table, made under Ferenc Braun the owner after 1811, is horseshoe shaped, and holds gilded wooden statues of Hygeia and Panacea, daughters of Asclepius, the god of healing. The pharmaceutical jars on the shelves are of various periods. About 160 wooden skillets, a dozen holders for powders and liquids with the initials “I.H.S.”, a brass mortar (with the inscription: “Apothecae S. J. Alba Regalensis Anno 1752”) and a tincture-press remain from the original mid-18th-century apothecary set.
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.short_description: The history of the Black Eagle Pharmacy in Székesfehérvár is associated with the Jesuit order. The Society of Jesus (SJ) considered the professional healthcare of the community as an integral part of its duty and established pharmacies in several Hungarian towns. Granted the right to operate a pharmacy in Székesfehérvár in 1745, the first pharmacy was established in the refectory of the old Jesuit monastery from 1746, for which Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop produced richly adorned wooden furniture in 1758. The furnishings were auctioned after the dissolution of the order in 1773, but did not go far, however, for Ferenc Walter purchased the furnishing for the Black Eagle Pharmacy that he opened across the street and which operated for 200 years.
af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, field work and restoration.

af30fe58-2fc8-572e-9e7e-11d4a4ed403b.history:
The Jesuit order settled in Székesfehérvár in 1688. The first pharmacy was opened in the town the same year and owned secularly up until 1745 with exclusive rights to run a pharmacy. The Jesuits then bought the rights, operating pharmacies in several Hungarian towns including Pozsony (Bratislava), Nagyszombat (Trnava), Trencsén (Trenčin), Eger, Győr and Kőszeg. Besides their devotion to providing healthcare in the local community, the order had extensive experience in pharmacy-management worldwide owing to their missionary activities in, for example, Europe and the Far East. The Jesuit Székesfehérvár pharmacy was established in the old monastery refectory in 1746, where Brother Joannes Maschner was apothecary until 1747. He was succeeded by Mathias Hyll who remained in the position from 1748 to 1774.  
The cabinetmaker, Bernát Baumgartner (SJ) and his workshop produced richly adorned wooden furniture for the Rococo-stuccoed pharmacy in the monastery refectory in 1758. In 1773, when the order was dissolved, the finely carved and gold encrusted apothecary’s unit, the table (since destroyed) and the pharmacy equipment were auctioned. The equipment did not go far, however, for Ferenc Walter purchased it for the Black Eagle Pharmacy that he opened across the street. After 1811, Ferenc Braun, the owner at that time, replaced the table with one in the Empire style. The secular pharmacy operated continuously until 1971 under several different owners. Recent restorations have revealed the original blue-green mottled surfaces of several wooden skillets with inscriptions in a Rococo cartouche frame. These, along with certain pieces of wooden furniture from the pharmacy laboratory, must have belonged to the furnishing of 1758 and are thought to be the works of József Codelli, a Jesuit convert and head of the furniture workshop between 1746 and 1747. A pharmacy museum was opened on the premises in 1973; since 1975 it has been known as the Black Eagle Pharmacy Museum.

b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.name: *Still Life with Fruit, Dead Birds and a Bowl of Morels*
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.description:
The area of the picture featuring a seasonal still life is packed with dead birds – coal tit, great tit, goldfinch, pigeon, woodpecker, woodcock – and fruit such as grapes, damsons and apples, the produce of the autumn harvest. As is common with similar decorative still life paintings, the fruits shown do not co-exist in nature: morels are among the earliest spring mushrooms. The composition axis is provided by a silver-plated gun in the diagonal. Attention is drawn to the centre of the painting by red tones, changing to olive-green towards the edges.  
Still life paintings made appealing decorations for chateau interiors as supraports, in dining halls, hunting rooms and studies. The Central European artists continued the tradition of Flemish still life established by Frans Snyders and Jan Fyt.  
This still life is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, a remarkable artist of Spanish origin. In 1698 he became a burgher of Brno and an active member of the painters' guild. He signed a proposal that painters and sculptors be articled, the first attempt to detach artists from the guild system, which was followed by efforts to establish an art academy in Brno by the artists Etgens and Eckstein. The majority of artworks to originate in Moravia in the second half of the 17th century were the work of foreign artists mainly Dutch and Italian, while work by Czech artists prevailed in the 18th century.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.short_description: The painting, reminiscent of 17th-century Dutch models, is the only known work by Coelestin Anctor Ximenes, an artist of Spanish origin who settled in Brno. The picture comes from the chateau of the High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma, in Brussels.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.method_for_datation: The picture is marked and dated *Ximenes fe. 1697*.
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.provenance: Collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau
b793ca61-b95f-58b2-ad32-809e29bedece.obtention: The picture comes from the collection of Count Salm-Reifferscheidt at the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau, where it remains to this day. The origins of the collection, which is dominated by Dutch painting, was associated with Antonín Karl Salm-Reifferscheidt (1720–1769), High Steward of Archduchess Marie Isabela of Parma in Brussels. Salm-Reifferscheidt also built the Rájec chateau, designed by Isidore Canevale.

c2204737-36b2-5b9a-90d0-d28e9ef48d69.name: Galleria del Senato
c2204737-36b2-5b9a-90d0-d28e9ef48d69.short_description: The gallery is 34 by 8.50 metres. The room faces Piazza del Nettuno and is located in the 15th century wing of the Palace which was designed by Fioravante Fioravanti, also known as the architect of the Kremlin in Moscow. The vault's decoration is an example of Bolognese prospective “Quadratura”. It is comprised of allegorical and heraldic figures regarding Bologna's history, its greatness,its government and its “Virtues”. This tecnique was brought to the rest of Europe and Latin America in the 17th century.
c2204737-36b2-5b9a-90d0-d28e9ef48d69.method_for_datation: According to the Diario Fava (a manuscript chronicle ) the room was inaugurated on the 20th of July 1677. A leaflet titled “*L'Elogio*” by Terisio Biondi (1677) tells us that the vault was first shown to the public on the 24th of August, during the *Festa della Porchetta* (the festival of the Roast Pork).

*Diario Fava*, Bologna, Archiginnasio Municipal Library, Ms. B. 33, c. 177.  
Roli, R., *Pittura Bolognese 1650-1800. Dal Cignani ai Gandolfi*, Bologna, 1977, pp. 245-46.

c2204737-36b2-5b9a-90d0-d28e9ef48d69.history: The gallery was commissioned around the spring of 1675 and was inaugurated on the 20th of July 1677. According to a leaflet published by Terisio Biondi in that same year, the room was opened to the public for the festival of 24th of August. In fact, on Saint Bartolomew's day the “Festa della Porchetta” (a festival organized by the Bolognese nobility) took place every year on the main square. From the “Anziani” balcony on the façade of the Palazzo Pubblico a roast pork (*Porchetta*) was thrown to the people. The same text provides a description of the allegorical figures and illustrates the great admiration of the population. Angelo Michele Colonna (1604–1687), who had already contributed to the Sala Urbana in the Palazzo Pubblico (commissioned in 1630 by the Bolognese Papal Legate Cardinal Bernardino Spada in honour of Pope Urbano VIII), was helped by the young Gioacchino Pizzoli (1651–1731).
c2204737-36b2-5b9a-90d0-d28e9ef48d69.patrons: The Senate of Bologna, the work was supervised by Count Filiberto Vizzani and Count Giuseppe Michele Malvasia

c43f2018-ad22-53fa-81fb-0f82619bafdc.name: The Town Hall of Augsburg
c43f2018-ad22-53fa-81fb-0f82619bafdc.description:
A special feature of the Augsburg Town Hall is the double-tower façade, an element that previously had been exclusively incorporated in churches. Other meaningful front decorations include the columned portal and the scrolled gable, which is equipped with two icons that signify the city’s imperial immediacy: the Roman cembra nut of the municipal coat-of-arms resting above and the double eagle of the Emperor's coat-of-arms in the centre.  
The spatial layout follows the models of Venetian palaces and is defined by the threefold division of the façade: The representative halls form the centre, beside them are administration and *Fürstenzimmer* spaces, in which the onion dome crowned towers surmount the staircases. Due to its hillside location, the building features seven single storeys facing forward and nine storeys in the rear.  
The middle section houses three halls that are staggered vertically according to their meaning: The ground floor is occupied by a vestibule, the so-called “Unterer Fletz”, a hall with marble pillars and a vaulted ceiling. Located in the first main storey is a secondary vestibule, also known as the “Oberer Fletz”, a once low coffered ceilinged hall with columns, whose adjacent rooms contained offices and assembly halls for the council body. Finally, on the second main storey is located the Golden Hall, the highlight of the building's interior design. This ceremonial hall features six portals, wall frescos, splendid coffered ceilings, and extends one row of windows and two clerestories high. Around the corners of the hall are four adjoined *Fürstenzimmer*.  
The allegoric iconography covering the walls and ceiling portray the Golden Hall’s concept as a conference site for the Diets of Augsburg, though such meetings never actually took place there. The ceiling centrepiece appellatively shows the triumphal procession of Sapientia (Wisdom); Latin inscriptions proclaim her motto: “By me rulers reign”. The centrepiece is flanked by two circular scenic tondos and eight oval-shaped paintings featuring female personifications. One of the circular paintings shows the Town Hall under construction and the architect holding the layout plan, to which the banner correspondingly says: “Cities are founded”. The required basic principles for the statement: education, productivity, diligence and piety are invoked by the four surrounding oval paintings. The other circular painting depicts Augsburg’s strength for defence, a banner says: “Foes will be fended off”. This, too, is surrounded by oval paintings, that allegorically visualise medicine, justice and prosperity. Wall frescos depict ancient Roman and German emperors.
c43f2018-ad22-53fa-81fb-0f82619bafdc.short_description: With development beginning in 1615, the double-towered town hall of the former free imperial city of Augsburg was a constructional pioneering achievement, because at that time it supposedly was the only building in the world with more than six storeys. Its form follows the models of Venetian palaces and the exquisite shapes of Italian Renaissance architecture. Expression of the municipal identity are the Roman cembra nut and the imperial double eagle residing exteriorly, as well as the magnificent Golden Hall with its splendid coffered ceiling interiorly. They symbolise the pride of the long history and immediacy of the city.
c43f2018-ad22-53fa-81fb-0f82619bafdc.method_for_datation: Archival documents and chronicle sources; portal inscription “MDCXX”

c43f2018-ad22-53fa-81fb-0f82619bafdc.history: In 1614, the dilapidated medieval town hall’s prestigious new construction was under consideration. The laying of the first stone was carried out by municipal architect Elias Holl on 25 August 1615. Due to a change of plans, two towers were added in 1618. Unfinished, the building was already in use in 1620, and the interior decoration was finalised six years later. In 1944, an air raid destroyed the building almost entirely, leaving only its external walls. After an initial simplified rebuilding, the showpiece of the town hall, the Golden Hall, and two of the original four *Fürstenzimmer* (literally “princely rooms”, similar to state rooms; spaces which served to receive German “Fürst”, or leaders of a feudal state) were reconstructed during a renovation between 1980 and 1984.

c57d333e-3668-5ecf-a874-92fe954d840d.name: Palazzo Ranuzzi (former Ruini and later Baciocchi)
c57d333e-3668-5ecf-a874-92fe954d840d.description:
Around 1680, the earl Marc'Antonio Ranuzzi (and after him his son Annibale) financed the decoration of many of the rooms of the palace. One of the ceilings, frescoed around 1680–1681 by the painter Marc'Antonio Franceschini and the quadratura painter Enrico Haffner, are well preserved. In the room alongside are frescoes painted in the same period by the brothers Giuseppe and Antonio Rolli. They also decorated an alcove, which, like other work by the painters Ercole Graziani and Tommaso Aldrovandini, mentioned by local historiographers, is now lost. Along with the construction of the monumental staircase we must also remember the decoration of another room on the main floor, realized by the painter Giovanni Andrea Seghizzi. This room contained paintings commissioned to Francesco Antonio Peruzzini, Giovanni Antonio Burrini and Sebastiano Ricci. These paintings were all dedicated to the illustrious ancestors of the Ranuzzi lineage.  
Another phase of the long artistic history of the building is connected with the patronages of Ferdinando Vincenzo Ranuzzi and Girolamo Ranuzzi. Ferdinando commissioned the still existing Great Hall, designed by the architect Ferdinando Galli Bibiena, with stuccoes made by Giuseppe Borelli and sculptures by Giuseppe Maria Mazza (1719). Girolamo commissioned the decoration of the ceiling of the so-called Galleria of the palace to the painters Vittorio Bigari and Stefano Orlandi (1724–1725).
c57d333e-3668-5ecf-a874-92fe954d840d.short_description:
If externally the palace is still noted for its definitively renaissance style, internally it is one of the more representative buildings of the Bolognese baroque and high baroque period. The main attraction is the monumental staircase, an astonishing and highly original structure based on a very dynamic conception of the space that was, and still is, considered an *unicum*.  
Other interesting aspects are the decorations completed in different periods in the main rooms of the building. We highlight in particular the fresco painted by Marc'Antonio Franceschini together with Enrico Haffner and the ceiling paintings of the so-called Galleria, created by Vittorio Bigari and Stefano Orlandi.  
The palace also housed an important collection of paintings in the past.
c57d333e-3668-5ecf-a874-92fe954d840d.bibliography: *Palazzo Ranuzzi Baciocchi. Sede della Corte d'Appello e della Procura Generale della Repubblica*, Bologna, 1994.
c57d333e-3668-5ecf-a874-92fe954d840d.history:
The architect of the palace is not known although local historiography recalls the illustrious name of Andrea Palladio. The construction of the palace of the noble Ruini family began after 1576. The work was still in progress in 1584, when the building was officially inaugurated in order to celebrate the election of the patron, Carlo Ruini, as senator of the city. The palace remained unfinished in 1679 when the Marquise Isabella Ruini, last heiress of the lineage, sold it to Earl Marc'Antonio Ranuzzi. Immediately, he financed new work and in 1680 as the building was nearly completed it was possible to start the interior decoration. When Marc'Antonio's son, Annibale, erudite and amateur of the arts, inherited the palace he commissioned new work too.  
In 1822 the palace was bought by Prince Felice Baciocchi, widower of Elisa Bonaparte. Today it hosts one of the city's courts of law.

c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.name: Triumphal Arch of Venetian General Leonardo Foscolo
c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.alternate_name: Slavoluk venecijanskog generala Leonarda Foscola; (Foscolo Arch)
c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.description: In essence, Foscolo Arch is a re-interpretation of a classical Roman triumphal arch, “embraced” by the older structure of Big Revelin, but lacking the autonomy characteristic of its antique predecessors. Composed of two superposed parts horizontally divided by a relatively thin cornice, the upper part consists of two flat pillars set wide apart from one another and crowned by a sort of cornice capital. This in turn supports a wide, decorative arch over an empty aedicule, which probably held a statue of General Leonardo Foscolo. The lower part, with the entranceway in the middle, is made of massive rustic stones arranged radially against the arch and flanked either side by two semi-columns.
c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.short_description: The Foscolo Arch is the biggest public monument in Korčula dedicated to a military commander of Venetian Dalmatia. Composed of two superposed parts divided horizontally by a thin cornice, the upper part consists of two flat pillars supporting a wide decorative arch over an empty aedicule: a statue of Venetian General Leonardo Foscolo probably once filled the void. The lower part, with the entranceway in the middle, is made of massive rustic stones arranged radially against the arch and flanked either side by two semi-columns.
c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.bibliography: Mohorovičić, A., “Gradovi u Hrvatskoj” in *Hrvatska i Europa. Barok i prosvjetiteljstvo*, sv. III., Zagreb, 2003, p. 586.
c8105e79-1640-585a-89d3-083c8be344d0.history: On the rear façade of the Tower of Big Revelin facing the Town Hall Square stands the Triumphal Arch of Venetian General Leonardo Foscolo. Incidentally, Big Revelin was built in the 13th century; it was enlarged again later and the last reconstruction took place in 2003. The Foscolo Arch is the biggest public monument in the city of Korčula dedicated to the military commander of Venetian Dalmatia, General Leonardo Foscolo. In the line of duty fighting in the Candian war (Kandijski rat, the war between the Turks and Venice 1645–1669 in Dalmatia, inland Dalmatia and Montenegro) he won battles against the Turks in Klis and Vrana and liberated a large part of the Dalmatian and Makarska coasts and Poljica.
keywords: Architecture, urban planning, triumphal arch, Baroque

caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.name: Parnassus Fountain
caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.description:
The fountain, made of Eggenberg limestone, consists of a triangular rock formation with a grotto inside, from which Hercules leads the three-headed dog, Cerberus, guardian of the underworld, in chains. The grotto is flanked by three female figures representing the ancient empires of Babylon, Greece and Persia. The composition is crowned by the figure of Europa as a symbol of the Holy Roman Empire and Christianity, and victor over the Anti-Christ. The basin of the fountain, shaped like a six-pointed rose, surrounds the rock formation on a stepped base with stone dolphins spouting water. Parnassus, a mountain near Delphi, is, according to Greek mythology, the seat of Apollo (whose statue students thought crowned the fountain) and is a symbol of inspiration.  
The subject of the fountain is water as a source of life and a symbol of purity, together with the ideals of good over evil and order over chaos seen in the context of the power of Christianity and the Habsburgian empire. With this fountain the City of Brno demonstrated its loyalty to the emperor while monumentalising its place within European history.
caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.short_description: The fountain is located in the second most important square in Brno. Although it acquired the name “Parnassus”, seat of the Muses, the fountain’s sculptures symbolise Europe and allegorise the ancient empires. The subject of the fountain is water as a source of life and a symbol of purity, together with the ideals of good over evil and order over chaos seen in the context of the power of Christianity and the Habsburgian empire. With this fountain the City of Brno demonstrated its loyalty to the emperor while monumentalising its place within European history.
caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.method_for_datation: In 1690 J. B. Fischer von Erlach signed a contract with the Brno Town Council. The date of completion in 1696 is recorded on the fountain.

caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.history: The fountain stands on the site of an earlier one of 1597 in the second most important square in Brno and at the intersection of one of the city’s main communication routes. Unfortunately, the majority of palaces that originally lined the square have not survived. The Reduta building is one of the oldest theatres in Central Europe; in 1767 the first performance in Czech was held there and 11-year-old Mozart played in the theatre. The old market (1293) demarcated the border between the parishes of St. Peter and St. James and linked the two city gates of Brno. Underneath the square is a dense network of storage cellars. The architect was anything but punctual and work on the fountain fell badly behind, complicating the lives of many of the citizens of Brno.
caa5e410-00c5-5c58-b735-1e71ea79346d.architects: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach (1656, Graz – 1723, Vienna), Tobias Kracker (1658, Vienna – 1736, Vienna), Anton Riga (around 1660, Kaliningrad – 1728, Brno)

cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.name: Fountain of the Acqua Paola
cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.description: In ancient Rome fountains placed at the end of an aqueduct used to be embellished with spectacular architectures such as *nymphaea,* trophies or *castella,* which celebrated the complex hydraulic venture that provided water to the *Urbe*. In 1587 Sixtus V had inaugurated the first modern fountain, which intended to recall, in terms of style and magnificence, the ancient models. This was the Mostra dell’Acqua Felice, also known as the Fountain of Moses, on the Quirinale Hill. The great fountain at the Janiculum Hill, in a dominant position over the city, located at the end of the Trajan aqueduct restored by Paul V, took the name of Mostra dell’Acqua Paola, from the name of the reigning pontiff. The architect Flaminio Ponzio, with the collaboration of Giovanni Fontana, was commissioned to direct the works, which were carried out between 1610 and 1612, reusing, among other things, ancient marbles from the Imperial Forums. The model of the tripartite triumphal arch takes up the architectural scheme of the Mostra dell’Acqua Felice but, unlike that, the Janiculum fountain has two additional narrower and lower arches on the sides and is also located in an isolated naturalistic context. This is emphasized by the openings that allow the view of a garden behind. The three arches, enclosed by semi-columns, support the large celebratory inscription that can be read just under the tympanum. This shows the papal coat of arms flanked by two angels sculpted by Ippolito Buzio.
cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.short_description: The “show-fountain”, imitating a triumphal arch, was designed by Flaminio Ponzio and Giovanni Fontana, dedicated to Pope Paul V Borghese. It celebrates the great undertaking of bringing water from the Lake of Bracciano (about 40 km away) to Rome.
cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.bibliography:
Rolfi, S., “Fontanone del Gianicolo”, *I principi della chiesa,* Milan: Edizioni Charta, 1998: 144.  
Tolomeo, M.G., “La mostra dell'acqua Paola”, in Pisani Sartorio, F. and Liberati Silverio, A. (eds) *Il trionfo dell'acqua: acque e acquedotti a Roma,* Rome: 1986: 250–254.
cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.history:
Since the Middle Ages, the Trastevere area was the least supplied with water in the whole city. In the early seventeenth century, due to Pope Paul V Borghese having sponsored the reactivation of the Trajan aqueduct (built in 109 AD), a new source of drinking water, coming from Lake Bracciano, 64 kilometres north of Rome, was made available to the people living in the Janiculum as well as to the populous district of Trastevere. To meet the expenses of this grandiose enterprise, the pontiff was forced to institute new taxes.  
Paul V also had another fountain inaugurated, located in front of the Hospice of Beggars, at the end of Via Giulia. Among his goals there was also that of rivalling Sixtus V, celebrated at the end of the sixteenth century for having the Felice Aqueduct repaired, thus providing water to the vast area of the Quirinale.
cc6b9c9c-7710-51e9-b60a-082edf0cd38c.architects: Flaminio Ponzio (architect); Giovanni Fontana (engineer); Ippolito Buzio (sculptor)

d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.name: Former residence of the painter family Zeiller
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.description: The paintings adorning the Zeiller House, in which Johann Jakob Zeiller had his home and workshop, are closer stylistically to the work of his cousin Franz Anton which is why they are usually attributed to the latter. It is an especially rich example of the “Lüftlmalerei” common in Außenfern. As Außenfern belonged to the diocese of Augsburg, the stylistic sources as well as pictorial models are primarily to be sought there. The special features of the paintings on the Zeiller House are their virtuoso composition featuring religious and profane motifs and exoticisms.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.short_description: The most famous of the numerous residential houses with façade paintings in Lechtal, Tyrol, was the home of the famous family of painters Zeiller. The façades of the elongated house are decorated on three sides with “Lüftlmalerei” (outside paintings), with the especially richly decorated gable end with bay window forming the main visible face. A very pretty example of the artistic self-presentation of this period.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.dates: The house with a gable-end façade was built in the 16th century and subsequently altered numerous times. The Late Rococo façade paintings originate from the period around 1770/75.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.bibliography: Baur-Heinhold, *Margarete, Süddeutsche Fassadenmalerei vom Mittelalter bis zur Gegenwart*, Munich 1952, pp. 114–18.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.history: The Zeiller House, also called “Schönes Haus”, was erected in the 16th century. It is situated in the north of Reutte on the so-called “Untermarkt” (Lower Market). It survived the major fires of 1703/04. Paul Zeiller (1658–1738), the father of Johann Jakob and founder of the Außerfern school of painting had his workshop here. On the south side of the building fragments of paintings are preserved which date from around 1600. The façade paintings on the other sides originate from around 1770/75 and are either the work of Johann Jakob or his nephew Franz Anton Zeiller.
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.architects: Façade paintings, attributed to: Franz Anton Zeiller (1716–1794) or Johann Jakob Zeiller (1708–1783)
keywords: Façade paintings; Lüftlmalerei; fresco paintings; secular building; residential house; family of artists
d097475a-8ad7-5263-8b4d-b1c5381c6516.author: Frank Purrmann

d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.name: Petar Zrinski  (Vrbovec, Croatia, 6.6.1621–Wiener Neustadt, 30.4.1671)
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.description:
A descendant of a noble and distinguished Croatian family, Count Petar Zrinski excelled in battles against the Turks. After the death of his elder brother Nikola (d. 1664) – Croatian *ban* (viceroy) and a most prominent Hungarian poet of his time – Petar became *ban* from 1665 to 1671. He translated – from Hungarian to Croatian – Nikola's poem *Adrianskoga mora Syrena* (The Siren of the Adriatic Sea). He was married to Ana Katarina Frankopan (d. 1673) with whom he had a son, Ivan Antun, and three daughters: Judita Petronila and Veronika who became nuns, and Jelena (1643–1693), who married first Franjo Rákóczy and later Emerik Tököly.  
Petar Zrinski along with other distinguished noblemen – his brother-in-law Franjo Krsto Frankopan, Franjo Nadasdy and Erasmus Tattenbach – were accused and tried for conspiracy against the Absolutist rule of Emperor Leopold I Habsburg. Found guilty, execution of the conspirators took place at Wiener Neustadt on 30 April 1671. On the eve of his death, Petar wrote a famous goodbye letter in Croatian to his wife Katarina, beginning with the words “My dear heart …” After his death the huge Zrinski estates in Croatia were confiscated and plundered.  
The portrait shows Petar Zrinski dressed as a wealthy nobleman, with the Zrinski coat of arms in the upper left-hand corner. Painted for the monastery in Svetice near Karlovac, Croatia, this portrait together with the portrait of Emperor Leopold I, are by an unknown Pauline artist. Pairing up the two portraits – *Petar Zrinski* and *Emperor Leopold I* – suggests that both were produced before the conspiracy and trial, some time before 1670.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.short_description: A portrait of the Croat nobleman, Count Petar Zrinski, who excelled in battles against the Turks and was executed for treason by Emperor Leopold I.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.initial_owner: Gallery of Donors, Pauline monastery in Svetice
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.method_for_datation: A painted inscription at the bottom of the work states “*Monastery Szveticzensis fundationem 1627. factam, Comes / Petrus Zrinius ratificat 1640. 19 Iuny. Eidémq(ue) forum Ecclesiae / Vicinum imperpetuat 1646*”, indicating that the painting was for the Pauline monastery in Svetice, Croatia. Further confirmation of the date and origin of the work relies on documentation in the Museum inventory.
d1d8cb50-1251-5dab-a6ce-97b1c120592b.obtention: Bought for the Museum from a private owner in 1964.

d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.name: *Anna Maria Victoria Jabornigg-Gamseneck*
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman in an ermine pelisse, she sits on a chair by a table on which are geometrical implements, several books and some sheets of paper.  
The painting is thought to be a portrait of Maria Victoria Jabornigg Gamsenegg, the first wife of Josip Ignac Sigismund Hilleprand-Prandau, son of Petar II Anton.  
Attributed to Ephraim Hochhauser who studied at the Vienna Academy and made his name painting portraits of the aristocracy, perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context. The woman holding compasses in her hand sits in front of sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.  
The History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum in Budapest has an identical portrait, which according to researchers represents Maria Christina the beloved daughter of Empress Maria Theresia, and attributed to the court painter Martin van Meytens who was a great favourite of the Empress. Since Petar II Hilleprand-Prandau was in the diplomatic service of the Austrian Court, it is possible that a portrait of the Empress's daughter found its way to Valpovo Manor.
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.short_description:
A portrait of a finely dressed and learned noblewoman, which according to the Prandau family archive, is a portrait of Anna Maria Victoria – the first wife of Josip Ignac – son of Petar II Anton.  
There is an identical portrait in the History Gallery of the Hungarian National Museum by Martin van Meytens, which according to researchers shows Maria Christina, daughter of Empress Maria Theresia.  
Perhaps the identity of the sitter in this case is less important than the context, for the woman holding compasses in her hand sits amidst sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and protractor. At the time, geometry was an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and seen as part of a good education. With a little freedom of thought, we might link these items with the laying out of the Baroque *parterre* garden in front of Valpovo Manor.
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.initial_owner: Valpovo, family of Baron Hilleprand-Prandau later of Count Normann-Ehrenfels
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.dates: Third quarter of the 18th century; about 1770
d367a154-49f9-5be0-a44e-c1259f9e26e2.obtention: Confiscated after the Second World War.

d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.name: *Portrait of Domenico Scarlatti*
d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.description:
Court Maestro to the exiled Polish queen Maria Kazimiera, and responsible for the Vatican's *Capella Giulia*, Domenico Scarlatti (1685–1757) was hired in 1714 as *Kappelmeister* by the Marquis of Fontes, Ambassador to King D. João V, at the Court of Pope Clement XI.  
Scarlatti's arrival in Portugal was a result of the high praise he had received from the King of Portugal's brother, Prince D. António who had attended one of his concerts in Rome. Scarlatti arrived in Portugal in around 1720 to become Princess Maria Barbara and Prince D. Jose's music teacher. Meanwhile the Pope had consented to the upgrade of the Royal Chapel to a Patriarchal Chapel and Scarlatti was invited to become *Kappelmeister* of the orchestra and choir of the Patriarchal Seminar Chapel.  
The Neapolitan Scarlatti's contribution to the Portuguese music scene was immense, he introduced Italian Opera, and the new musical and artistic patterns in vogue all over Europe at the time.  
In 1729 Scarlatti moved to Madrid to become once again Princess Maria Bárbara's music master, who by this time had married the Prince of Asturias, son of King Philip V and future King Philip VI of Spain. He remained in Spain until his death in 1757.  
Under the patronage of King D. João V, Domenico Scarlatti lived with his family in Spain where he enjoyed all the preconditions necessary to enhance his musical career and ensure his notoriety grew among his European musical peers.  
The art of portraiture peaked in the 18th century, fuelled by commissions from the European monarchs. Artists such as Louis Michel Van Loo, court painter to King Philip V of Spain (grandson of Louis XIV) between 1738 and 1752, or Jean Ranc (1674–1735) gained notoriety. The latter also painted the Portuguese Royal family following H. Rigaud.  
So it was that the Spanish artist Domingos António Velasco painted this portrait of Scarlatti in the Van Loo style in around 1739. Velasco depicts the maestro standing in front of an opulently painted curtain, his body twisted to the right and his hand resting on a wooden box. The light falls on the musician's face and hands, and he is dressed in a golden yellow and grey-blue ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious St James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.
d435d9f4-9833-55f4-b40f-d413ab1c10be.short_description: *Kappelmeister* of the Patriarchal orchestra and choir, and music master to Princess Maria Barbara the daughter of the King D. João V and the Queen of Spain, this portrait of Domenico Scarlatti is by the Spanish painter Domingos António Velasco. The artist depicts Scarlatti dressed in a ceremonial court vestment, adorned with the prestigious Order of St. James, a cognizance bestowed upon him one year previously by King D. João V, Grand-Master of the Order.

d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.name: *The Gourmet*
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.description:
Jacob van Schuppen studied painting with his father – Pierre Louis van Schuppen a painter and engraver in Antwerp – and his uncle, Nicolas Largillière, one of the period's most respected portrait painters. This beginning determined both his career and his preferred genre. Van Schuppen worked both in Paris and at the Lorraine princely court in Luneville as a portrait painter. In 1705, he became a member of the Paris Academy, arriving in Vienna in 1716 as a successful and notable portraitist in the service of Prince Eugene of Savoy. Having been settled in the imperial city for only a short time, he became court painter in 1723. In 1725, he approached the emperor with a plan for a French-style art academy, which he directed from 1726. Vienna's Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture (Academy of Fine Arts Vienna) was unprecedented in Central Europe and remained the most important institution of its kind in the German-speaking territories. As a painter, van Schuppen was primarily an excellent portraitist. His large-size portraits, representing the aristocracy and contemporary writers and artists, effectively reflect the personality and character of the sitters.  
*The Gourmet*, although for a long time registered as a work of a German master, is an excellent example of van Schuppen's art, holding the characteristic features of his work. Like his other paintings, the motifs of both genre painting and still life are present.  
The objective approach of Dutch and Flemish art, fine colouring and French elegance come together in this painting; the basic motif – a man uplifting his glass to demonstrate his aspirations in seeking happiness in drinking and smoking: the minor pleasures of life – is a favourite and frequent characteristic of 17th-century painters. Although known primarily as a portraitist, van Schuppen nevertheless approached genre painting in a similar way, as can be seen in this painting and others in Hungarian collections.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.short_description: Jacob van Schuppen, from the Netherlands, was a pupil of his uncle Nicolas Largilliere. From 1716 he lived in Vienna, and from 1726 directed the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, breathing new life into the institution, which was renamed the Imperial and Royal Court Academy of Painters, Sculptors and Architecture. *The Gourmet*, showing a man enjoying the finer things of life, is both a portrait and a genre painting.
d6484564-de31-5ad5-b6c7-ba70506e3e5f.obtention: Initially from the Esterházy Collection in Pottendorf, in 1867 Endre Pánthy acquired the painting. From 1906, it was in the Lyceum school’s substantial collection in Eger as part of the Endre Pánthy legacy. It was then transferred to the Dobó István Castle Museum in Eger.

d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.name: *Ships in a Harbour*
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.description: A finely executed Baroque painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. The composition is a rare example of a small size genre piece, which may have been part of a series. The execution of the painting is finely detailed, and contrary to its small size, the work is of high quality. This is an unusual representation within the iconography of this type of picture. Scenes of everyday life became common in the 17th and 18th centuries, and depictions of the “low-life” of peasants and the “high-life” of the aristocracy, featuring fashionably dressed figures in different scenes were also common. The popularity of seascapes and maritime pictures spread to Hungary by way of Flemish and Dutch painting. Small seascapes (*zeekens*) were a very popular theme representing – like this painting – imaginary views of exotic ports.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.short_description: A finely executed Baroque genre painting of a harbour with ships and throngs of people on the shore. Because of these and other features, the painting represents a rare example among Baroque seascapes.
d74f35ca-a39e-5420-b35a-7c0303499e61.obtention: From the bequest of Count Jenő Zichy in 1903.

da8131c4-37b0-5710-a8a7-07aeac9637d5.name: Mughal Cabinet
da8131c4-37b0-5710-a8a7-07aeac9637d5.description:
During the first half of the 16th century, the Indian sub-continent was confronted by two new foreign presences: the Portuguese, who had dominion over the coastal regions and, in the north, the forces that would later become the vast empire of the Mughals. Among the Mughal Emperors, Akbar (r. 1556–1605) stands out. He consolidated his rule and, having gained stability and subsequently reorganised the imperial finances, he demanded from his workshops creations of extraordinary quality. Akbar understood the complex reality of India with its roots in both Hindu and Islamic traditions. The imperial workshops, therefore, produced hybrid objects to reflect this reality, but also revealed the strong artistic influences of the Portuguese missionaries (namely the Jesuits), and of the Chinese and European merchants. Such were Akbar's curiosity and interest in the Christian religion of the Portuguese and their art, that he requested the civil and ecclesiastical authorities in Goa to send a Jesuit mission to his court. A refined artistic style resulted from this fusion, seen not only in paintings but also in textiles, metalwork, clothing and furniture.  
This magnificent piece of furniture takes as its prototype Portuguese cabinets which had inspired those made in Goa. The decoration and the materials used are, however, from Mughal sources. The front of the cabinet is inlaid and symmetrical in 12 sections; each section a drawer decorated with human figures among vegetation in either courtly scenes or with animals. The doors are decorated with the Tree of Life, among which branches are mythical birds and elephants. Significantly, beneath, are Portuguese figures – indicated by their clothing – hunting on horseback with long lances.  
This cabinet clearly shows the crossover between cultures and illustrates the luxurious items available among the European courts.
da8131c4-37b0-5710-a8a7-07aeac9637d5.short_description: The term Mughal defines the dynasty founded in 1526 by Babur in Northern India and also signifies objects produced by the imperial workshops where several influences from different areas of the empire and from Portuguese missionaries combined. Based on Portuguese cabinets made in Goa, the material and the decoration are typically Mughal. Significantly, on the bottom of the doors, Portuguese figures – indicated by their clothing – are hunting on horseback with long lances.

e0fae875-b47c-5739-af86-c73b563c01c5.name: Downtown Lisbon
e0fae875-b47c-5739-af86-c73b563c01c5.description:
The plan of *Baixa Pombalina* was conceived by Manuel da Maia and Eugénio dos Santos, while Carlos Mardel and others provided the simple, symmetrical and harmonised prototype designs for the building façades. Based on an octagonal-grid system with parallel and perpendicular streets of various sizes, *Baixa Pombalina* covers an area that stretches from the River Tejo and Praça do Comércio, in the south, and Rossio and Praça da Figueira in the north.  
The Praça do Comércio is a quadrangular structure based on a U-shaped plan. It has three uniform façades and a ground-level arcade that terminates in two large pavilions overlooking the river on the fourth side. Access to the river is through the Cais das Colunas (Columns Quay). The bronze equestrian statue of King José I by Machado de Castro is dominant in the middle of the square. In front of the statue on the north side, a 19th-century triumphal arch by Veríssimo José da Costa and his team, leads to the urban centre.
e0fae875-b47c-5739-af86-c73b563c01c5.short_description: In the aftermath of the destruction caused by the earthquake of 1755, downtown Lisbon was rebuilt to comply with the innovative and pragmatic principles of Enlightenment urban planning and architecture. It was named after the Marquis of Pombal, who coordinated the reconstruction together with his team of architects and engineers. With an octagonal grid-shaped plan, regular and symmetrical facades stretching from the Praça do Comércio to Rossio make this area both historically and culturally significant; Praça do Comércio is classified as a National Monument and *Baixa* as a National Heritage Site.
e0fae875-b47c-5739-af86-c73b563c01c5.bibliography:

França, J.-A., *A Reconstrução de Lisboa e a arquitectura Pombalina*, ICP, Lisbon, 1978.  
Calado, M., Ferreira, V., *Lisboa*, Lisbon, 1992.  
Tostões, A., *Catálogo Exposição Lisboa 1758, o Plano da Baixa hoje*, Lisbon, 2008.
e0fae875-b47c-5739-af86-c73b563c01c5.history:
On 1 November 1755 a violent earthquake, followed by a tsunami and a week-long fire, destroyed two-thirds of Lisbon. Around 10,000 people were killed and the most important part of the city was in ruins. Terreiro do Paço (the Palace square and commercial centre situated by the river), the 16th century palace of King Manuel I (remodelled by King Philip II of Spain and embellished by King Joao V), the Casa da India (Royal Emporium), close to the Alfândega (Customs) and Arsenal (Navy), several churches (including the Patriarchal Basilica), hospitals, the Opera and the upper class area were all destroyed.  
With a square that opens up onto the river, a new urban solution was conceived.  The Marquis of Pombal co-ordinated the rebuilding programme, reaffirming architecturally the absolute power of the king with the principle governmental and administrative buildings, a triumphal arch and, at its centre, an equestrian statue of King José I.

Calmels (1822–1906)

e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.name: *Portrait of Historian, Márton György Kovachich*
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.description:
Messerschmidt was born in south-west Germany. After studying in Munich and Graz, he matriculated at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna in 1755. Having graduated, he was employed at the Imperial Arms collection. During the period 1760–69 his work followed the artistic style of the Late Baroque court, at that time under the determining influence of Balthasar Ferdinand Moll. From 1769, Messerschmidt's first Neo-Classical works appear and to which he applied the experiences of his study trip to Rome in 1765. In 1770–72, Messerschmidt began to work on his so-called *Character Heads*, obviously connected with certain paranoid ideas and hallucinations from which, at the beginning of the 1770s, the master began to suffer. After an unsuccessful application to the office of a leading professor at the Academy, in 1777, he settled down in Pozsony (Bratislava) where he dedicated himself primarily to his *Character Heads* and in addition made other portraits as well.  
The bust of Márton György Kovachich (1743–1821), a historian, a custodian of the Buda university library, and one of the most eminent scholars of the Enlightenment in Hungary, was the last of these commissions in Messerschmidt's oeuvre. Kovachich commissioned the portrait directly from the artist in Pozsony (Bratislava), a fact corroborated by a letter from Kovachich dated 1 May 1783, at which time the portrait was already standing in his room in Buda. Like the *Character Heads* the bust is made in the early Neo-Classical style preferred by Messerschmidt since 1769–70. His works of this period have an accentuated plainness, but nevertheless have a vigorous modelling and structure. The portraits have a timeless, monumental character enhanced by their firm portraiture, one marked by the face-on portrayal of his subject. These stylistic characteristics of the Neo-Classical aesthetic are, however, coupled with an exact portrayal of the sitter's features, so that Messerschmidt's portraits remain very close to a realistic appraisal of human individuality.
e608c729-04c2-56e1-b2e3-0064a245a0ed.short_description: Messerschmidt moved to Vienna and later to Pozsony (Bratislava) from Bavaria. He made his famous *Character Heads* in Pozsony (Bratislava) when he was mentally ill. All of them portray the features of the artist. The bust of the historian, Kovachich, was made by the artist at a time when he his mental health was good.

e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.name: *Holy Trinity Column in Buda*
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.description:
In the 17th and 18th centuries, different types of Holy Trinity statues reminded people of the sufferings of the plague of 1691. The Holy Trinity Column in Buda, standing in front of the Parish Church of the Holy Virgin and the Old Town House of Buda, was built between 1710 and 1714. In 1916, during World War I, the column was the scene of the coronation of king Charles IV Habsburg. The column was demolished at the end of the 19th century.  
The original copperplates for this engraving are also preserved in the museum's collection. There were nine statues on the monument altogether, all of which were carved by Fülöp (Philipp) Ungleich. The three reliefs and coat-of arms were made by Antal (Anton) Hörger. Later, 16 statues were added to the column. The architectural setting surrounding the column also changed several times. During World War II the original statues in the collection of the Budapest History Museum were seriously damaged. A smaller size engraving was also made of the monument decades later.
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.short_description: A large-size Baroque engraving representing the Holy Trinity Column, one of Buda’s most precious Baroque monuments.
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.method_for_datation: On the basis of the work and its inscription
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.obtention: Transferred from the Capital’s collection in 1945

e7f75235-a225-5c2d-8277-f6319d17a9f3.name: The Servite Monastery Church of St. Charles Borromeo
e7f75235-a225-5c2d-8277-f6319d17a9f3.description: The central space of the St. Charles Church is a domed square with a round chapel adjoining to the east, south and north respectively. The design is based on the idea of the unity of the Trinity, which is also repeated in the chancel tower with its trefoil ground plan. To the west a transverse vestibule connects to the two later chapels. While the exterior is in the style of the Early Baroque, the interior is dominated by that of the Late Rococo.
e7f75235-a225-5c2d-8277-f6319d17a9f3.short_description: The St. Charles Church in Volders is one of the most interesting buildings of its time and the first Baroque centralised building in north Tyrol. It was built by a dilettante architect who venerated the Holy Trinity, symbolically incorporating it into the building design. While the exterior still displays the exotic looking ornamental forms of the period of its construction, the interior has been redesigned in the style of the late Rococo with monumental ceiling paintings from Martin Knoller.
e7f75235-a225-5c2d-8277-f6319d17a9f3.bibliography:
Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 33f.  
Bodner, R. M., *Die Karlskirche in Volders*, Volders 1988.  
Petersohn, S., “Die Karlskirche in Volders. Die Herkunft der Bauformen und ihre Bedeutung für den frühbarocken Kirchenbau nördlich der Alpen”, in: *Veröffentlichungen des Tiroler Landesmuseums Ferdinandeum*, 79, 1999, pp. 33–54.
e7f75235-a225-5c2d-8277-f6319d17a9f3.history: The church and monastery were designed and donated by the municipal physician of the city of Halle, Hippolytus Guarinonius, on the occasion of the plague year of 1611. The foundation stone was laid in 1620, the consecration was held in 1654 (St. Charles Borromeo and the Holy Trinity). Further chapels were built in 1670 and 1710. The redesign of the interior with Knoller’s ceiling frescos was completed in 1765/66. Last restored in 1977-88.

e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.name: Villa Pucić
e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.description:
Villa Pucić is characterised by a square ground plan. The load-bearing walls are directed inwards, linking the rear and front elevations, and dividing the space into three elongated parts. The central part – occupied by the lobby on the ground floor and the main hall on the first floor – rises up into the roof space (the belvedere) and runs the entire depth of the building. The terraces meanwhile connect the central part with the sides at first-floor height, giving volume and contour, articulated in steps. To these longitudinally directed main rooms, the transversal axis of the two-flight staircase at the side contrasts with the heightened staircase vestibule, opened up with arches, on the ground floor. On the first floor, the division of the basic spatial units into smaller rooms contributes to the complexity of the space, divided around three sides of the central façade hall. A particular feature of the building is its barrel-vaulted utility areas below the terrace, and the division of the ground floor into a commercial front elevation and a residential rear elevation, in part oriented to the walled garden.  
The interior furnishing does not lag behind the unique organisation and ground plan of the building, with composite columns on the staircase and rich Rococo stuccowork in the main hall and surrounding residential rooms. The exterior is also highly distinctive, for along with the aforementioned terraces and belvedere, sequences of balustrades run along the edges of the terrace, while volutes flank the belvedere on either side.  
With these features, the Pucić residence echoes on one hand the Baroque residential architecture that took shape in Dubrovnik after the earthquake, and on the other hand presents considerable innovation. The stylistic continuation of the architectural tradition of the city can be seen in the organisation and furnishing of the staircase – done in the style of a grand city palace – but also in the style of an out-of-town villa. The side terraces, designed to add volume to the body of the palace and inspired by Dubrovnik Cathedral, are an element introduced by the architect, Tommaso Napoli (active 1689–1700). Considering its southern Italian (Sicilian) origins, it is not surprising that the Villa Pucić with its terraces has direct parallels in southern Italian architecture (Masseria Cartesia in Apulia). An almost identical approach was used by the neo-Palladian architect, Giorgio Massari, in the Villa Tamagnino Lattes in Istrana near Treviso (1715). This heterogeneous pedigree makes it difficult to answer the question of who the architect might have been, the more so that in the second half of the 18th century there were no significant foreign architects at work in Dubrovnik (as there were after the 1667 earthquake). Hence, the notion is plausible that the owner of the palace, making use of his position in the diplomatic service, might have commissioned the design abroad and then confided it to a local Dubrovnik builder, who perhaps would have had some experience in nearby Boka Kotorska, which was also rich in similarly conceived Late Baroque villas.
e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.short_description: Villa Pucić, built in the immediate vicinity of the Pile Gate, represents, in the framework of Baroque residential architecture in Dubrovnik, a building of the highest quality. Organised axially with one wing and two floors, the reception rooms are at the centre and run the entire depth of the building, rising up to the first floor. The influences of Venetian architecture, as seen here, are also present in the nearby Boka Kotorska. The side terraces, however, reflect those of Dubrovnik Cathedral and, accordingly, southern Italian architecture.
e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents and stylistic features.
e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.bibliography:
Marković, V., “Kuća i prostor grada u Dubrovniku nakon potresa 1667 godine”, in *Radovi Instituta za povijest umjetnosti* 14, 1990, pp. 137–149.  
Horvat-Levaj, K., *Barokne palače u Dubrovniku*, Zagreb–Dubrovnik, 2001, pp. 171–177.  
Horvat-Levaj, K., “Između ljetnikovaca i palača – reprezentativna stambena arhitektura dubrovačkog predgrađa Pile u 18. Stoljeću” in *Kultura ladanja - Zbornik radova sa znanstvenih skupova »Dani Cvita Fiskovića« održanih 2001. i 2002 godine*, Zagreb, 2006, *pp*. 203–220.
e836da75-e025-5b3f-991c-d69329392311.history: Written sources confirm that Matej Pucić’s villa existed in the Dubrovnik suburb of Pile in 1760. Built in the immediate vicinity of the City Gate known as Pile Gate, it is thought that the land was vacant in 1760, and it is reasonable, therefore, to suggest that Villa Pucić was designed and built by an unknown architect during the Late Baroque period.

e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.name: Telč
e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.description:
The square is lined with picturesque houses with gables and arcades closed off by the chateau to the west. The historical core and original layout of the houses have been preserved each with a width of 8–10 m and a depth of around 30 m. Entering from the square a mighty stone gateway opens into a vaulted vestibule, a “*mázhaus*”; the gateway of which takes up almost two-thirds of its width. The *mázhaus* is used for the sale of handicrafts and beer. There are stairs leading to the cellar and upper floors, and a passageway to the yard and garden.  
A number of houses are decorated with Renaissance *sgraffiti* – intricate patterns or images scratched out in wet plaster – and most of them have frontages segmented with relief ornamentation, ledges and niches. They are crowned with volute gables and straight roofs, sometimes with parapet semi-floors, decorated with relief spheres, cones, vases and figurative motifs. The uniform effect is facilitated by blind windows.
e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.short_description: The square is an example of a modern urban concept, an effort to create a compact whole. Its multicoloured architecture and decorative sculptures resemble theatre props, creating a space for everyday life. The unique complex of Renaissance and Baroque houses has been included in the UNESCO World Heritage List.
e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.method_for_datation: A great many architectural elements feature stonemasons’ marks and dates. For example, the portal of the Jesuit College is dated 1654. The construction of the Plague Column is dated by the donor’s will and by the contracts with the sculptor and stonemasons in charge. Individual building projects were mainly determined by historical events and projects initiated by demesne owners.
e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.bibliography:
Vlasta Kratinová – Bohumil Samek – Miloš Stehlík, *Telč, historické město jižní Moravy,* Prague, 1992  
Miroslav Plaček, *Hrady a zámky na Moravě a ve Slezsku*, Prague, 1999, pp. 339–341.
e9289d0f-8e02-5bd6-9690-3b3e03583c21.history: The town of Telč grew up around a royal homestead founded in the 13th century at the crossroads of busy trade routes. Its present appearance dates from the second half of the 16th century, when the chateau was rebuilt as the seat of the Moravian provincial governor, Zachariáš of Hradec. The arcades and house frontages were constructed to a uniform design. After his death, the town lost the status of feudal seat and became part of the Jindřichův Hradec demesne. Its owner, Vilém Slavata, was one of the victims of Prague Defenestration in 1618. During the Thirty Years’ War the town was plundered by the imperial army under Albrecht of Valdštejn and again in 1645 by the Swedes. It became the governor’s seat again under F. A. Liechtenstein-Castelkorn, whose enterprises launched the reconstruction of the town houses. In 1992 the historic heart of Telč was included in the UNESCO World Heritage List.

e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.name: House of Pilate
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.alternate_name: Pilatushaus, residence of the mayor, Anton Lang
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.description:
Two façades of the Pilatushaus must be emphasised because of their symbolically valuable biblical scenes which are virtuously integrated into the real architecture of doors and windows. The effect is supported by the depiction of shadows, almost perfectly blending the *trompe l'oeil* with the real features of the building, in order to trick the observer.  
The south façade of the house, also known as the garden side, seems to have a round portico supported by columns above and before the entrance door. Two painted stairways lead up on both sides of the portico to pedestals on which human figures are displayed, which are commonly termed as pharisees. Between these pedestals, Pontius Pilate is sitting on a throne, where, at his feet, there is a kneeling Jesus Christ. It is assumed that the owner of the house took part in the local Passion play in the role of Pontius Pilatus, thus possibly giving the house its name. Typically Baroque architectural elements, along with floral and figural forms, frame the images.  
The gable of the east side of the house shows a Resurrection scene in a shell-shaped niche between two windows. On the balcony one can find the fleeing keepers of the grave. The figure on the right is leaping over the balustrade in an alarmed, but slightly unnatural movement. The two lower zones of the façade are decorated exclusively with painted architectural elements and seem to be separated from the gable zone by a cornice. This side of the building is dominated by illusionist architectural painting of the balcony, the cornice, the window frames, diverse arrangements of columns, a coat-of-arms in a cartouche and other such ornamental elements. The clever use of perspective layering invokes an interpretation pointing towards Baroque theatre architecture.
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.short_description: The Pilatushaus is one of the main works of Franz Seraph Zwinck, the so called “Lüftlmaler”, and also a unique example of the special kind of facade painting named after him that is so typical for Upper Bavaria. The “Lüftlmalerei” is characterised by stunning *trompe l'oeil* and mostly religious scenes that have symbolic value. Based on Italian models, the style spread throughout the towns and rural areas of Bavaria.
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.bibliography:
Lorch, J., “Die Malereien am Pilatushaus”, in Koch, L. et al, *Franz Seraph Zwinck. Der Lüftlmaler von Oberammergau*, Oberammergau 1986, pp. 92–9, 105.  
Rattelmüller, P. E., *Lüftlmalerei in Oberbayern*, Munich 1981, pp. 72–4.
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.history:
Franz Seraph Zwinck created the illusionistic architectural decoration of the Pilatushaus in 1784. Due to restorative works – by Franz Hartmann in 1910 and Ludwig Magnus Hotter in 1960 – the facade painting is no longer in all parts in its original state. To rectify this, another restoration took place between 1985 and 1986.  
At the time the façade paintings were created, the house was owned by Anton Lang who was one of the most famous long-distance traders of private devotional carvings typical in Upper Bavaria at the time.  
One can assume that the patrons of such “Lüftlmalerei” were wealthy citizens who were aware of the arts and wanted to express their confidence and status. The painted houses can thus be interpreted as prestige objects for the owner.
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.patrons: Mayor and long-distance trading merchant, Anton Lang
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.architects: Facade painting: Franz Seraph Zwinck (1748–1792) also known as “Lüftlmaler”
keywords: Lüftlmalerei; façade painting; fresco; *trompe l'oeil*
e93b7ba8-0d78-59b6-8156-1ad29cc582c8.author: Heidi Thiede

e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.name: Palazzo Doria Pamphili, frescoes
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.description:
Following acquisition of the estate, the majestic restructuring of the palace began immediately, and by 1657, the extensive decorative scheme for the rooms on the main floor was in progress. Four large rooms on the south side are known as Fire, Air, Water and Earth on account of the representations in them, and four smaller rooms on the other side contain images of the Four Continents (Africa, America, Asia and Europe) around the larger, rectangular Prince’s room, whose walls show a landscape opening onto a colonnade that supports a balustrade. At the centre of the vault in the Prince’s room the coat of arms of Pamphili Aldobrandini is clearly commemorative.  
Two more rooms intended for religious services display religious subjects. Many painters from different places were involved in the decorative scheme, all inspired by Cortona. First there is the Fire Room, created by Cozza between 1658 and 1659, with a continuous representation of Vulcan’s Forge, entirely free of architectural divisions. Next, the Air Room, the masterpiece of the cycle, painted in just 16 days by Preti in 1661 where the subject is rendered perfectly through the sense of “airiness” that pervades the entire composition, which shows allegories of *Dawn*, *Day*, *Evening* and *Night*. The Water Room, painted between 1658 and 1659 by Cortese, has four side panels and one central panel, divided by monochrome telamons that hold up *trompe-l’oeil* architecture, with mythological subjects related to Water. The similarly laid out Earth Room was painted by Tassi between 1657 and 1659, and is divided by pairs of caryatids with a personification of the Earth at its centre. In the smaller rooms, America and Africa have been attributed to Mola, Asia to Cozza, and Europe to Tassi, while the Prince’s Room was decorated by Dughet and Borgognone between 1658 and 1659.
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.short_description: The decoration consists of four large rooms on the south side of the building known as Fire, Air, Water and Earth on account of the representations in them, and four smaller rooms on the other side with images of the Four Continents (Africa, America, Asia and Europe) around the larger, rectangular Prince’s room. The entirety can be understood to be an extensive decorative scheme inspired by Cortona and intended to celebrate the family in space (the continents) and in time (the elements of human life).
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.bibliography:
Baiocchi, G. and Indrio, L., “Palazzo Doria Pamphili”, *I Principi della Chiesa*, Milan 1998, pp. 191–3.  
B. Fabjan and M. Di Gregorio (eds) *Palazzo Doria Pamphilj a Valmontone*, Rome 2004 (with bibliography).
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.history: The Valmontone estate was acquired by Camillo Pamphili, nephew of Pope Innocent X Pamphili (1644–55), in 1651, with the aim of undertaking a grand restructuring project for the entire village (the Pamphiljan Town) which was to be centred round the palace, the church and the square. The Pamphili family, from a small Umbrian patriciate, had lived in Rome since the 15th century and found recognition of its social ascent in particular with the appointment to the papacy of Giovanni Battista as Innocent X. A series of significant urban development projects, which can be dated to the mid-17th century, still characterise both the city of Rome and the surrounding area: including the palace in Piazza Navona, the palace on the Corso acquired through the marriage of Camillo and Olimpia, the Casino del Bel Respiro in the out-of-town villa San Pancrazio, and the ambitious restructuring program for the village of Valmontone.
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.patrons: Camillo Pamphili (1622, Naples – 1666, Rome), cardinal and nephew of Pope Innocent X, son of Olimpia Maidalchini, put aside the purple cloth to marry Olimpia Aldobrandini
e9cb69db-be9f-5174-b7c3-5166bd5a0783.architects: Guillaume Courtois (Cortese) known as Borgognone (1628–79) of French origin, in Rome around 1640, pupil of Pietro da Cortona; Francesco Cozza (1605–82), from Calabria, in Rome from 1631; Gaspard Dughet (1615–75), of a French father and brother-in-law of Nicolas Poussin, landscape artist who often worked with Courtois; Pier Francesco Mola (1612–66), born in Ticino but in Rome since childhood; Mattia Preti (1613–99), from Calabria, in Rome from the 1630s, active in Valmontone in 1661 just before leaving for Malta, where he died; Giambattista Tassi, the least well-known, between 1657 and 1681
keywords: Fresco, allegorical, commemorative, decoration, *trompe-l’oeil*
